statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be a prime, let m\ge1, and put k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let X and Y be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \mathbb F_{q^m}. Suppose that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge0 and on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge0. Then it is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge0.
proof:
Let q=p^a, \ell\neq p, m\ge 1 and k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q be as in the statement. Put q' := q^{m} = p^{am}. Then q' is a prime power with the same residue characteristic p, so \ell\neq p still holds, and \overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}=k. Let \sigma:k\to k be the field automorphism \sigma(c)=c^{q'}=c^{q^{m}}. For a scheme Z over \mathbb F_{q'} we write F_Z := (\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* for the q^{m}-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); this is exactly the operator appearing in the statement of the lemma. The varieties X and Y of the statement are smooth projective geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^{m}}=\mathbb F_{q'}, and the product in the statement is X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y with base change to k.

Fix n\ge 0. We prove that F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y} is semisimple on H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 1 (K\"unneth decomposition, Frobenius-equivariantly). Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 with the prime power q' = p^{am} in place of q (all its hypotheses are met: q' is a prime power, \ell\neq p, and X, Y are smooth projective over \mathbb F_{q'}, while k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}). It gives that for every n\ge 0 the Q_\ell-linear map
\Phi_n:\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad x\otimes y\mapsto \operatorname{pr}_1^*x\cup\operatorname{pr}_2^*y,
is an isomorphism of Q_\ell-vector spaces, and that under \Phi_n the operator F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y} corresponds to the block-diagonal operator \bigoplus_{i+j=n}\bigl(F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)}\bigr), where F_X^{(i)} denotes F_X acting on H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and F_Y^{(j)} denotes F_Y acting on H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Explicitly,
\Phi_n\circ\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i+j=n}F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)}\Bigr)=F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y}\circ\Phi_n.  (1)

Step 2 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of the factors). Since X_k and Y_k are proper over the algebraically closed field k, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (applied with q' in place of q and with the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell, which carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) shows that H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell for all i,j\ge 0. Moreover, by lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (again with q' in place of q), F_X^{(i)} and F_Y^{(j)} are Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of these spaces, hence F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)} is an automorphism of the (i,j)-summand.

Step 3 (semisimplicity of each tensor summand). By hypothesis, F_X^{(i)} is semisimple on H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and F_Y^{(j)} is semisimple on H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), for all i,j\ge 0. The field K:=\mathbb Q_\ell has characteristic 0, the spaces involved are finite-dimensional and the operators are invertible. Hence lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_590 applies and yields that
F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)} is semisimple on H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
for every pair (i,j) with i+j=n.

Step 4 (semisimplicity of the block-diagonal direct sum). The index set \{(i,j)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{2}: i+j=n\} is finite and nonempty (it contains (n,0)), so the direct sum in Step 1 is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional Q_\ell-vector spaces, and each summand operator F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)} is invertible (Step 2) and semisimple (Step 3). By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9, the direct-sum operator
T_n:=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)}
is semisimple on V_n:=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^{i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 5 (transport along the K\"unneth isomorphism). By Step 1, \Phi_n:V_n\to H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a Q_\ell-linear isomorphism and, by (1), it intertwines the invertible operators T_n and F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y}. Applying lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 with V:=V_n, W:=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), T_V:=T_n, T_W:=F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y} and \alpha:=\Phi_n, we conclude that F_{X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y} is semisimple on H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q'}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Since n\ge 0 was arbitrary, the q^{m}-power arithmetic Frobenius (\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^{m}}, is semisimple on H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{m}}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0, as claimed. (No connectedness of the product is needed anywhere: geometric connectedness of X and Y over \mathbb F_{q^{m}} is only used to match the hypotheses of the statement, and the K\"unneth isomorphism of lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 requires only smoothness and projectivity.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be a prime, let m\ge1, and put k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \mathbb F_{q^m}, let E be a vector bundle of rank r+1\ge1 on Y defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and let \pi:\mathbb P(E)\to Y be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. Suppose that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge0. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P(E)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge0.
proof:
Proof. Put q' := q^m = p^{am}. Then q' is a prime power with ℓ ≠ p = char(F_{q'}), and k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}. The variety Y is smooth projective geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q'}, the vector bundle E of rank r+1 ≥ 1 is defined over \mathbb F_{q'}, and π: P(E) → Y is the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients; in particular P(E) is smooth projective, hence proper, over \mathbb F_{q'}. Fix once and for all a nonzero element of \mathbb Q_ℓ(1) and use it to identify Tate twists with \mathbb Q_ℓ; this is the normalization under which lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_569 is stated.

Throughout, F_Y denotes the q'-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{Y_k} × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^{q'}, on H^*_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ), and F_P denotes the q'-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{P(E)_k} × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^{q'}, on H^*_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ). Since q' = q^m, these are exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius operators appearing in the statement of the lemma. We use the convention H^j_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) = 0 for j < 0 (and, as is true by dimension vanishing, also for j > 2 dim Y).

For each integer n ≥ 0 set
  V_n := ⊕_{i=0}^{r} H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ),
and let T_n : V_n → V_n be the block-diagonal operator whose i-th block is q'^i F_Y : H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) → H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ).

Step 1 (projective bundle formula with Frobenius). The hypotheses of lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_569 are satisfied with q' in place of q: q' = p^{am} is a prime power, ℓ ≠ p = char(\mathbb F_{q'}), k = \overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}, Y is smooth projective geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q'}, E is a vector bundle of rank r+1 ≥ 1 on Y defined over \mathbb F_{q'}, and π is the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients. Its conclusion gives, for every n ≥ 0, a \mathbb Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism
  Φ_n : H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) → V_n = ⊕_{i=0}^{r} H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ)
such that
  (1)  Φ_n ∘ F_P = T_n ∘ Φ_n,
where T_n acts on the i-th summand as q'^i F_Y = q^{mi} F_Y.

Step 2 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility). (a) Y is proper over \mathbb F_{q'}. Applying lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with q' in place of q, with X = Y, and with K = \mathbb Q_ℓ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, shows that H^j_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_ℓ for every j ≥ 0. Hence V_n, a finite direct sum of the finitely many spaces H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) for 0 ≤ i ≤ r, is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_ℓ. (b) P(E) is proper over \mathbb F_{q'}; the same lemma applied to X = P(E) shows that H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_ℓ. (c) By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a applied with q' in place of q and X = Y (respectively X = P(E)), the operators F_Y and F_P are \mathbb Q_ℓ-linear automorphisms of the respective cohomology spaces; in particular they are invertible. Since q'^i = p^{ami} ≠ 0 in \mathbb Q_ℓ (a field of characteristic 0), each block q'^i F_Y is invertible, hence so is the block-diagonal operator T_n.

Step 3 (each block is semisimple). Fix i with 0 ≤ i ≤ r and put V_{n,i} := H^{n-2i}_ét(Y_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ). If n-2i < 0, then V_{n,i} = 0, and the unique operator on it is semisimple and invertible vacuously. If n-2i ≥ 0, then by the hypothesis of the lemma F_Y is semisimple on V_{n,i}; by Step 2(a) V_{n,i} is finite-dimensional and by Step 2(c) F_Y is invertible. Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248, applied with V = V_{n,i}, T = F_Y and c = q'^i ∈ \mathbb Q_ℓ^×, then shows that the scalar multiple q'^i F_Y is semisimple on V_{n,i}. (The conclusion is of course trivial when V_{n,i} = 0.)

Step 4 (T_n is semisimple). By Step 3, for each i = 0, ..., r the block q'^i F_Y is a semisimple invertible \mathbb Q_ℓ-linear operator on the finite-dimensional space V_{n,i}. Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (with m = r+1, V_j = V_{n,j-1} and T_j = q'^{j-1} F_Y for j = 1, ..., r+1) therefore shows that the direct sum T_n = ⊕_{i=0}^{r} q'^i F_Y on V_n = ⊕_{i=0}^{r} V_{n,i} is semisimple. (For zero summands the operator is the identity on the zero space, which is semisimple, so the lemma applies without exception.)

Step 5 (transport to P(E)). Define
  α := Φ_n^{-1} : V_n → H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ).
This is a \mathbb Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism because Φ_n is one (Step 1). Starting from (1), namely Φ_n ∘ F_P = T_n ∘ Φ_n, multiply on the left by Φ_n^{-1} and on the right by Φ_n^{-1}. Using Φ_n^{-1} ∘ Φ_n = id and Φ_n ∘ Φ_n^{-1} = id, we obtain F_P ∘ Φ_n^{-1} = Φ_n^{-1} ∘ T_n, that is,
  (2)  α ∘ T_n = F_P ∘ α.
Now apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 with
  V = V_n,  W = H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ),  T_V = T_n,  T_W = F_P,  α = Φ_n^{-1} : V_n → W.
All its hypotheses are verified: V and W are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_ℓ-vector spaces (Step 2), T_V = T_n and T_W = F_P are invertible (Step 2), α : V_n → W is a \mathbb Q_ℓ-linear isomorphism (Step 1), and α ∘ T_V = T_W ∘ α is exactly (2). Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 therefore yields that F_P is semisimple on H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) if and only if T_n is semisimple on V_n. Since T_n is semisimple by Step 4, F_P is semisimple on H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ).

Conclusion. The operator F_P is exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{P(E)_k} × Spec σ)^*, σ(c) = c^{q^m}, on H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ). Since n ≥ 0 was arbitrary, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_ét(P(E)_k, \mathbb Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0, which is the assertion of the lemma. (Semisimplicity of an invertible operator over \mathbb Q_ℓ is equivalent to diagonalizability after extension of scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_ℓ, the formulation used in the conjecture; the quoted lemmas, in particular lemma_8, lemma_9 and lemma_248, are stated in exactly this sense. Moreover, since F_P is invertible, F_P is semisimple if and only if F_P^{-1} is: if the minimal polynomial of F_P is ∏(t-λ_j) with distinct nonzero λ_j, then the minimal polynomial of F_P^{-1} is ∏(t-λ_j^{-1}), again with distinct roots. Hence the corresponding statement for the geometric Frobenius follows as well.) ∎

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be a prime, let m\ge1, and put k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let X and Y be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimensions d_X and d_Y over \mathbb F_{q^m}. For Z\in\{X,Y\}, let H_Z be a very ample divisor on Z defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, let \xi_Z\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) be its cycle class under a fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell, and let L_Z be cup product with \xi_Z; suppose that L_Z^{d_Z-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d_Z-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0\le n\le d_Z. Let \xi=\operatorname{pr}_1^*\xi_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), the cycle class of the very ample divisor \operatorname{pr}_1^*H_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*H_Y, and let L be cup product with \xi. Then L^{d_X+d_Y-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2(d_X+d_Y)-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0\le n\le d_X+d_Y.
proof:
Proof. Put q' = q^m = p^{am}; then q' is a prime power and k = \overline{\mathbb F_{q'}}. Regard X and Y as smooth projective varieties over \mathbb F_{q'}, of pure dimensions d_X and d_Y respectively.

Step 1 (graded cohomology). For every integer r >= 0 set V_r := H^r_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and W_r := H^r_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). The k-scheme X_k is projective and equidimensional of dimension d_X, and Y_k is projective and equidimensional of dimension d_Y. Hence, by lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension, V_r = 0 for r > 2d_X and W_r = 0 for r > 2d_Y. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied with q' in place of q and with K = \mathbb Q_\ell (the constant sheaf, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism), each V_r and W_r is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. Thus V := \bigoplus_{r=0}^{2d_X} V_r and W := \bigoplus_{s=0}^{2d_Y} W_s are finite-dimensional graded \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.

Step 2 (Lefschetz operators). Let L_X: V -> V be cup product with \xi_X, and let L_Y: W -> W be cup product with \xi_Y. Since \xi_X \in H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and \xi_Y \in H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), we have L_X(V_r) \subseteq V_{r+2} and L_Y(W_s) \subseteq W_{s+2}. By hypothesis, L_X^{d_X-r}: V_r -> V_{2d_X-r} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= r <= d_X, and L_Y^{d_Y-s}: W_s -> W_{2d_Y-s} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= s <= d_Y.

Step 3 (tensor-product Hard Lefschetz). Apply lemma_tensor_product_lefschetz with K = \mathbb Q_\ell, m = d_X, n = d_Y, V, W, L_V = L_X, L_W = L_Y. Let T := L_X \otimes \mathrm{id}_W + \mathrm{id}_V \otimes L_Y \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V \otimes W), and grade V \otimes W by (V \otimes W)_t := \bigoplus_{r+s=t} V_r \otimes W_s. The lemma gives: for every integer t with 0 <= t <= d_X+d_Y, the map T^{d_X+d_Y-t}: (V \otimes W)_t -> (V \otimes W)_{2(d_X+d_Y)-t} is an isomorphism.

Step 4 (Künneth isomorphism). By lemma_146 applied with q' = q^m in place of q, for every n >= 0 the Künneth map \kappa_n: (V \otimes W)_n = \bigoplus_{i+j=n} H^i_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \otimes H^j_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) -> H^n_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times_{\mathbb F_{q'}} Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \alpha \otimes \beta \mapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta, is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. (Here \mathrm{pr}_1, \mathrm{pr}_2 are the projections of X \times_{\mathbb F_{q'}} Y.)

Step 5 (compatibility of L with T). Let L: H^*_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times_{\mathbb F_{q'}} Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) -> H^{*+2}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times_{\mathbb F_{q'}} Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) be cup product with \xi = \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X + \mathrm{pr}_2^*\xi_Y. We claim that for every n >= 0, L \circ \kappa_n = \kappa_{n+2} \circ T. It suffices to check this on a pure tensor \alpha \otimes \beta with \alpha \in H^i_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and \beta \in H^j_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), i+j=n. Using bilinearity, associativity and graded commutativity of the cup product, and the fact that \mathrm{pr}_1^* and \mathrm{pr}_2^* are ring homomorphisms, we compute: L(\kappa_n(\alpha \otimes \beta)) = (\mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta) \cup (\mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X + \mathrm{pr}_2^*\xi_Y) = \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta \cup \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X + \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\xi_Y. In the first summand, \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta has degree j and \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X has degree 2, so graded commutativity gives \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta \cup \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X = (-1)^{2j} \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta = \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta; hence \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta \cup \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X = \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_1^*\xi_X \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta = \mathrm{pr}_1^*(\alpha \cup \xi_X) \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta. In the second summand, associativity and the ring-homomorphism property of \mathrm{pr}_2^* give \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\xi_Y = \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*(\beta \cup \xi_Y). Therefore L(\kappa_n(\alpha \otimes \beta)) = \mathrm{pr}_1^*(\alpha \cup \xi_X) \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*\beta + \mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha \cup \mathrm{pr}_2^*(\beta \cup \xi_Y) = \kappa_{n+2}((\alpha \cup \xi_X) \otimes \beta + \alpha \otimes (\beta \cup \xi_Y)) = \kappa_{n+2}((L_X \otimes \mathrm{id}_W + \mathrm{id}_V \otimes L_Y)(\alpha \otimes \beta)) = \kappa_{n+2}(T(\alpha \otimes \beta)). This proves the identity on pure tensors; since pure tensors span (V \otimes W)_n, linearity gives L \circ \kappa_n = \kappa_{n+2} \circ T for every n \ge 0. (Here and below L^r denotes the r-fold iterate of L, i.e. cup product with \xi^r.)

Step 6 (iteration). We prove by induction on r \ge 0 that L^r \circ \kappa_n = \kappa_{n+2r} \circ T^r for every n \ge 0. For r=0 this is the identity \kappa_n = \kappa_n. If it holds for r, then, using Step 5 with n+2r, L^{r+1} \circ \kappa_n = L \circ (L^r \circ \kappa_n) = L \circ \kappa_{n+2r} \circ T^r = \kappa_{n+2r+2} \circ T \circ T^r = \kappa_{n+2(r+1)} \circ T^{r+1}.

Step 7 (conclusion). Fix an integer n with 0 \le n \le d_X+d_Y and put r := d_X+d_Y-n \ge 0. By Step 6, L^r \circ \kappa_n = \kappa_{2(d_X+d_Y)-n} \circ T^r. Since \kappa_n is an isomorphism (Step 4), composing on the right with \kappa_n^{-1} gives L^r = \kappa_{2(d_X+d_Y)-n} \circ T^r \circ \kappa_n^{-1}. By Step 3, T^r: (V \otimes W)_n \to (V \otimes W)_{2(d_X+d_Y)-n} is an isomorphism. By Step 4, \kappa_n and \kappa_{2(d_X+d_Y)-n} are isomorphisms. Hence L^{d_X+d_Y-n} = L^r is a composite of isomorphisms, so it is an isomorphism H^n_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to H^{2(d_X+d_Y)-n}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). This is the required assertion.

The argument also covers the cases d_X=0 or d_Y=0: lemma_tensor_product_lefschetz allows m,n \ge 0, and for a zero-dimensional smooth projective geometrically connected variety the cohomology is \mathbb Q_\ell in degree 0 and vanishes in positive degrees, so the same composite-isomorphism argument applies verbatim. (When d_X=d_Y=0, only n=0 occurs and the conclusion is the identity map.)

Remark. The very ampleness of \operatorname{pr}_1^*H_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*H_Y is not needed in the argument; only the given Hard Lefschetz isomorphisms for the two factors and the identification \xi=\operatorname{pr}_1^*\xi_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*\xi_Y are used.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(d\ge2\) be an integer, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Suppose that for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Y\) of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\). Then for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(X\) of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\) with \(n\neq d\).
proof:
Proof. Fix an integer m ≥ 1 and a smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. We must show that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F := (id_{X_k} × Spec σ_m)^*, where σ_m(c) = c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0 with n ≠ d.

Step 1: A smooth ample divisor over a finite extension. Since X is projective over F_{q^m}, choose a closed immersion X → P^N_{F_{q^m}} and let L be the restriction of O(1); then L is an ample line bundle on X defined over F_{q^m}. Apply lemma_306 with the prime power q^m in place of q, to the variety X and the ample line bundle L. The hypotheses of lemma_306 hold: d ≥ 2 and X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. We obtain integers s ≥ 1 and N ≥ 1 and a section t ∈ H^0(X_{F_{q^{ms}}}, L^{⊗N}) whose zero scheme Y := V(t) is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X_{F_{q^{ms}}}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d−1 over F_{q^{ms}}.

Put X' := X_{F_{q^{ms}}}. Then X' is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^{ms}}: it is the base change of X along the finite separable extension F_{q^m} → F_{q^{ms}}, so smoothness, projectivity and pure dimension d are preserved, and geometric connectedness holds because X'_k = X_k is connected. Moreover, there is a canonical identification X'_k = (X ×_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^{ms}}) ×_{F_{q^{ms}}} k = X ×_{F_{q^m}} k = X_k, and under this identification the q^{ms}-power arithmetic Frobenius on X'_k, namely (id_{X'_k} × Spec σ_{ms})^* with σ_{ms}(c) = c^{q^{ms}}, corresponds to F_{ms} := (id_{X_k} × Spec σ_{ms})^*. Similarly Y_k := Y ×_{F_{q^{ms}}} k.

Step 2: Lefschetz restriction maps. Y is nonempty because it is smooth of pure dimension d−1 ≥ 1 over F_{q^{ms}}, and Y is a proper closed subscheme of X' because dim Y = d−1 < d = dim X'. Base changing to k, Y_k is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor in X'_k = X_k, smooth of pure dimension d−1 over k: the section t pulls back to a section t_k of the ample line bundle (L_{F_{q^{ms}}})^{⊗N} on X_k whose zero scheme is Y_k, and t_k is a regular section because t is regular and k is flat over F_{q^{ms}}; ampleness is preserved by base change. Apply lemma_420 to the algebraically closed field k, the prime ℓ (ℓ ≠ p = char k), the smooth projective geometrically connected k-variety X_k of pure dimension d ≥ 2, and the divisor Y_k contained in X_k. Its conclusion is that the restriction map i^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for every integer n < d−1 (equivalently, for 0 ≤ n ≤ d−2) and is injective for n = d−1.

Step 3: Semisimplicity on the divisor. Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d−1 over F_{q^{ms}}: it is a closed subscheme of the projective F_{q^{ms}}-scheme X', hence projective, and it is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d−1 by Step 1. Since ms ≥ 1, the hypothesis of the lemma applies with m' := ms and with Y in place of X (whose dimension is d−1). It gives that the q^{ms}-power arithmetic Frobenius F_{ms,Y} := (id_{Y_k} × Spec σ_{ms})^*, σ_{ms}(c) = c^{q^{ms}}, is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0. Note that here we use the hypothesis of the lemma, which gives semisimplicity on all of H^n(Y_k), including the middle degree n = d−1; we do not use the target in dimension d−1, which would exclude that degree.

Step 4: Semisimplicity on X away from the middle degree. Apply lemma_429 with the prime power q^{ms} in place of q, with X' in place of X, with Y contained in X' as above, and with the same ℓ and k (note that k, the algebraic closure of F_q, is also an algebraic closure of F_{q^{ms}}). The hypotheses of lemma_429 are satisfied: (a) X' is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d ≥ 2 over F_{q^{ms}}; (b) Y is an effective ample divisor defined over F_{q^{ms}}, smooth of pure dimension d−1; (c) the restriction i^*: H^n(X'_k, Q_ℓ) → H^n(Y_k, Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for 0 ≤ n ≤ d−2 and injective for n = d−1, by Step 2 and X'_k = X_k; (d) the q^{ms}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n(Y_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0, by Step 3. Lemma_429 therefore yields that F_{ms} = (id_{X_k} × Spec σ_{ms})^* is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≠ d. (The statement of lemma_429 covers all integers n ≠ d, including n > 2d where the cohomology vanishes.)

Step 5: Descent from the q^{ms}-power to the q^m-power. Finally apply lemma_596 with q replaced by the prime power q^m, with X (over F_{q^m}) in place of its X, with the integer s ≥ 1 in place of its m, and with the same ℓ and n. Note that k, the algebraic closure of F_q, is also an algebraic closure of F_{q^m}. The lemma says that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F = (id_{X_k} × Spec σ_m)^*, σ_m(c) = c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) if and only if the (q^m)^s = q^{ms}-power arithmetic Frobenius F_s = (id_{X_k} × Spec σ_{ms})^* is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). Indeed, σ_{ms} = σ_m^s, so F_s = F^s, and semisimplicity is unaffected by replacing an operator by a positive power. By Step 4, F_s is semisimple for every n ≠ d. Hence F is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0 with n ≠ d.

Since m ≥ 1 and X were arbitrary, the lemma is proved.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be a prime, let m\ge1, and put k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d\ge2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, let Y\subset X be a nonempty very ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_{q^m} that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and let i:Y\hookrightarrow X be the closed immersion. Let \xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) be the cycle class of Y under a fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell, put \xi_Y=i^*\xi, and let L_X and L_Y be cup product with \xi and \xi_Y. Suppose that L_X^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0\le n\le d. Then L_Y^{d-1-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-2-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0\le n\le d-1.
proof:
Let H^n(Z) denote H^n_et(Z_k,Q_l). Fix a nonzero element u in Q_l(1) and use it to identify Q_l(r) with Q_l by u^r -> 1. Let tr_X and tr_Y be the Poincare duality traces under this identification, normalized compatibly as in lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor; changing both traces by the same nonzero scalar does not affect perfectness. We prove the assertion for each n with 0 <= n <= d-1.

First suppose n = d-1. Then L_Y^{d-1-n} = L_Y^0 = id on H^{d-1}(Y), hence is an isomorphism.

Now suppose 0 <= n < d-1. Put e = d-1, so e >= 1. Recall that X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d, and Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension e, both over F_{q^m}. By lemma_420 applied to X_k and Y_k (Y is a nonempty smooth ample Cartier divisor on X of pure dimension d-1, and n < d-1), the pullback i^*: H^n(X) -> H^n(Y) is an isomorphism.

We need a very ample divisor on Y with class xi_Y. Since Y is a very ample divisor on X, O_X(Y) is very ample over F_{q^m}. Hence O_Y(Y) = O_X(Y)|_Y is very ample on Y over F_{q^m}. Choose a nonzero section s in H^0(Y,O_Y(Y)) over F_{q^m} and let D = div(s). Because Y is positive-dimensional projective and O_Y(Y) is very ample, D is nonempty; and O_Y(D) is isomorphic to O_Y(Y), so D is a very ample divisor defined over F_{q^m}. Its cycle class is cl(D) = c_1(O_Y(Y)) = i^* c_1(O_X(Y)) = i^* xi = xi_Y.

Define B_X on H^n(X) by B_X(x,y) = tr_X(L_X^{d-n}x cup y). By hypothesis L_X^{d-n} is an isomorphism, hence injective. Applying lemma_448 to X with the very ample divisor Y and the integer n (0 <= n < d-1 <= d) shows that B_X is a perfect pairing.

Define B_Y on H^n(Y) by B_Y(a,b) = tr_Y(L_Y^{d-1-n}a cup b). We compare B_Y with B_X. For x,y in H^n(X), since xi_Y = i^* xi, we have L_Y^{d-1-n}(i^*x) = i^*(L_X^{d-1-n}x). Therefore
B_Y(i^*x,i^*y) = tr_Y(L_Y^{d-1-n}(i^*x) cup i^*y)
= tr_Y(i^*(L_X^{d-1-n}x) cup i^*y)
= tr_Y(i^*(L_X^{d-1-n}x cup y)).
Let z = L_X^{d-1-n}x cup y. Since x,y have degree n, z lies in H^{2d-2}(X). By lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor applied to the pair (X,Y) over F_{q^m}, the Gysin map i_! satisfies i_!(i^*w) = w cup xi for every w in H^*(X). Taking w=1_X in degree 0 gives i_!(1_Y) = xi. The defining property of i_! then gives, for z in H^{2d-2}(X),
tr_X(i_!(1_Y) cup z) = tr_Y(1_Y cup i^*z) = tr_Y(i^*z).
Hence tr_Y(i^*z) = tr_X(xi cup z). Substituting z gives
B_Y(i^*x,i^*y) = tr_X(xi cup L_X^{d-1-n}x cup y)
= tr_X(L_X^{d-n}x cup y)
= B_X(x,y).
Since i^*: H^n(X) -> H^n(Y) is an isomorphism and B_X is perfect, this identity shows that B_Y is perfect as well.

Now apply lemma_448 to Y, of pure dimension e=d-1, with the very ample divisor D (whose class is xi_Y) and the integer n (0 <= n <= d-1). Since B_Y is perfect, the map L_Y^{d-1-n}: H^n(Y) -> H^{2d-2-n}(Y) is injective. Finally, apply lemma_hard_lefschetz_reduces_to_injectivity to Y over F_{q^m} with the ample line bundle O_Y(Y) (whose cycle class is xi_Y) and the same integer n. Injectivity of L_Y^{d-1-n} implies that it is an isomorphism.

This covers all 0 <= n <= d-1, so the proof is complete.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \ell\neq p be a prime, and put k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let A be an abelian variety over \mathbb F_q. Then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius (\operatorname{id}_{A_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, where \sigma(c)=c^q, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge0.
proof:
Setup and notation. Fix a prime power q = p^a, a prime ℓ ≠ p, and k = F̄_q. Let σ : k → k be the q-power automorphism σ(c) = c^q, and for a scheme Z over F_q write F_Z = (id_{Z_k} ×_{Spec F_q} Spec σ)^* for the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on H^*_ét(Z_k, Q_ℓ). Let g = dim(A) ≥ 0. The goal is to show that F_A is semisimple on H^n_ét(A_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0.

Step 1 (structural facts about A). An abelian variety over F_q is by definition a geometrically connected, smooth, proper group variety over F_q; it is projective (this is part of the definition in the convention where abelian varieties are required to be projective, and otherwise it is the theorem that every abelian variety is projective). Hence A is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension g over F_q. Also A is nonempty, since it has the origin 0 ∈ A(F_q).

Step 2 (the case g = 0). If g = 0, then A is a geometrically connected finite étale F_q-scheme of degree 1 with a rational point (the origin), hence A ≅ Spec F_q. Base changing to k gives A_k ≅ Spec k. For the one-point scheme Spec k one has H^0_ét(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = Q_ℓ and H^n_ét(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = 0 for all n ≥ 1 (cohomology of a geometric point with constant coefficients). On H^0_ét(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = Q_ℓ the operator F_A is the identity: F_A is the pullback along a morphism of Spec k to itself, and pullback of the constant function 1 (the canonical generator of H^0) is again 1. The identity operator on the 1-dimensional space Q_ℓ is semisimple (its minimal polynomial is x − 1, which is squarefree). On H^n_ét(Spec k, Q_ℓ) = 0 for n ≥ 1 every operator is semisimple (the only invariant subspace of the zero space is 0, which has the complement 0; equivalently the minimal polynomial is 1, which is squarefree). Thus the claim holds for g = 0.

Step 3 (the case g ≥ 1: a generically finite cover by a product of curves). Assume now g ≥ 1. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_463_abelian_variety_covered_by_product_of_curves (with the same q and A, of dimension g ≥ 1). It provides smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1, …, C_g over F_q together with a proper surjective generically finite morphism
  f : C_1 ×_{F_q} ⋯ ×_{F_q} C_g ⟶ A
over F_q. Note that r := g ≥ 1 is a legitimate integer for the statement below, and no relation between r and dim(A) is required.

Step 4 (applying the generically-finite-descent lemma). We apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_584 with the following data, and check its hypotheses one by one:
  • q = p^a is a prime power and ℓ ≠ p is a prime: fixed as above; k = F̄_q.
  • X := A. By Step 1, A is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d := g over F_q. (Geometric connectedness holds because A has the F_q-rational origin, so A_k is connected, indeed irreducible.)
  • r := g ≥ 1, and C_1, …, C_g are smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_q: supplied by Step 3.
  • f : C_1 ×_{F_q} ⋯ ×_{F_q} C_g → A is a proper surjective generically finite morphism over F_q: supplied by Step 3.
All hypotheses of lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_584 are therefore satisfied. Its conclusion is exactly the assertion we need: the q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{A_k} × Spec σ)^*, where σ(c) = c^q, is semisimple on H^n_ét(A_k, Q_ℓ) for every integer n ≥ 0. This is the operator F_A of the statement.

Step 5 (conclusion, and the geometric Frobenius). Combining Steps 2 and 4, F_A is semisimple on H^n_ét(A_k, Q_ℓ) for every n ≥ 0, for every abelian variety A over F_q, which proves the lemma.

Remark (equivalence with diagonalizability over Q̄_ℓ, and the geometric Frobenius). Since Q_ℓ has characteristic 0, a Q_ℓ-linear operator on a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial is squarefree, and this property is unchanged after extending scalars to Q̄_ℓ (a squarefree polynomial stays squarefree over an extension of fields of characteristic 0, and an operator with squarefree minimal polynomial is diagonalizable over any splitting field). Hence the semisimplicity proved above is equivalent to the diagonalizability of F_A on H^n_ét(A_k, Q_ℓ) ⊗_{Q_ℓ} Q̄_ℓ asserted in the conjecture. Moreover, by the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, the geometric Frobenius (id_{A_k} × Spec σ^{-1})^* equals F_A^{-1}; since the minimal polynomial of T^{-1} is the reciprocal polynomial of the minimal polynomial of T, which is squarefree whenever T is invertible with squarefree minimal polynomial, the geometric Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_ét(A_k, Q_ℓ) as well.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let \beta:V\times V\to K be a K-bilinear form such that \beta(x,x)\neq0 for every nonzero x\in V, let c\in K^\times, and let F\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V) satisfy \beta(Fx,Fy)=c\,\beta(x,y) for all x,y\in V. Then F is semisimple.
proof:
Let \(V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,K)\). If \(V=0\) the assertion is trivial, so assume \(V\neq0\).

1. Nondegeneracy of \(\beta\). Define \(\Phi:V\to V^*\) by \(\Phi(v)(w)=\beta(w,v)\). If \(\Phi(v)=0\), then in particular \(\beta(v,v)=0\), hence \(v=0\) by the hypothesis. Thus \(\Phi\) is injective; since \(\dim_K V<\infty\), it is an isomorphism. In particular the right radical of \(\beta\) is zero.

2. Orthogonal complements of \(F\)-stable subspaces. Let \(U\subseteq V\) be an \(F\)-stable \(K\)-subspace and put \(U^\perp=\{v\in V:\beta(u,v)=0\text{ for all }u\in U\}\). We claim that \(V=U\oplus U^\perp\) and that both summands are \(F\)-stable.

First, \(U^\perp\) is \(F\)-stable: if \(v\in U^\perp\) and \(u\in U\), then
\[
\beta(u,Fv)=c\,\beta(F^{-1}u,v)=0,
\]
because \(F^{-1}u\in U\). (This uses \(\beta(F(F^{-1}u),Fv)=c\beta(F^{-1}u,v)\).)

Second, \(U\cap U^\perp=0\): if \(x\in U\cap U^\perp\), then \(\beta(x,x)=0\), so \(x=0\).

Third, \(\dim_K U^\perp=\dim_K V-\dim_K U\). Indeed, consider \(\Psi:V\to U^*\), \(\Psi(v)(u)=\beta(u,v)\). Its kernel is \(U^\perp\). It is surjective: any linear functional on \(U\) extends to a linear functional on \(V\), and since \(\Phi:V\to V^*\) is an isomorphism, every linear functional on \(V\) is of the form \(w\mapsto\beta(w,v)\) for some \(v\in V\). Hence \(\dim_K U^\perp=\dim_K V-\dim_K U\).

Therefore \(V=U\oplus U^\perp\). Since \(F\) is invertible and preserves \(U\), it also preserves \(U^\perp\), and the decomposition is \(F\)-stable.

3. The minimal polynomial \(m_F\) of \(F\) is squarefree. Suppose not. Then there is a monic irreducible \(p\in K[t]\) and an integer \(e\ge2\) such that \(p^e\mid m_F\). Write \(m_F=p^e q\) with \(q\in K[t]\) and \(\gcd(p,q)=1\). Let \(U=\ker p(F)\). We first note that \(U\neq0\). If \(U=0\), then \(p(F)\) is injective, hence invertible, and from \(0=m_F(F)=p(F)^e q(F)\) we get \(q(F)=0\), contradicting the minimality of \(m_F\) because \(\deg q<\deg m_F\). Thus \(U\neq0\). The subspace \(U\) is \(F\)-stable because \(p(F)\) commutes with \(F\).

By (2), \(W:=U^\perp\) is an \(F\)-stable complement: \(V=U\oplus W\).

On \(U\), \(p(F)=0\), so the minimal polynomial \(m_U\) of \(F|_U\) divides \(p\). Since \(U\neq0\), \(m_U\neq1\), hence \(m_U=p\).

On \(W\), the map \(p(F)|_W\) is injective: if \(w\in W\) and \(p(F)w=0\), then \(w\in U\cap W=0\). Hence \(p(F)|_W\) is invertible. From \(0=m_F(F)=p(F)^e q(F)\) on \(W\), multiplying by the inverse of \(p(F)^e|_W\) gives \(q(F)|_W=0\). Thus the minimal polynomial \(m_W\) of \(F|_W\) divides \(q\) (with \(m_W=1\) if \(W=0\)).

Since \(V=U\oplus W\) is an \(F\)-stable direct sum, \(m_F=\operatorname{lcm}(m_U,m_W)\). Hence \(m_F\mid \operatorname{lcm}(p,q)=pq\), because \(\gcd(p,q)=1\). But \(p^e q=m_F\) with \(e\ge2\) cannot divide \(pq\). This contradiction shows that \(m_F\) has no repeated irreducible factor; i.e. \(m_F\) is squarefree.

4. Conclusion. Since \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), every irreducible polynomial over \(K\) is separable. Factor \(m_F=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i\) into distinct monic irreducibles. The Chinese remainder theorem for the \(K[t]\)-module \(V\) gives
\[
V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r \ker p_i(F).
\]
On each summand \(p_i(F)=0\), and over an algebraic closure \(\overline K\) the polynomial \(p_i\) splits into distinct linear factors. Hence \(F\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline K\), i.e. semisimple. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open complement. Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\). Suppose that \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\). Let \(F=(\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) with \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\). If \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F\) is semisimple on \(P^d\).
proof:
Let us fix notation. Put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and let \(\sigma_m\) denote the \(q^m\)-power automorphism \(c\mapsto c^{q^m}\) of \(k\). Throughout, \(F\) denotes the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\); via the evident base changes it acts on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (all cohomology below is \(\ell\)-adic with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients, and \(U=X\setminus Y\)). Let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) and \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be the inclusions. Note that \(q^m=p^{am}\) is again a prime power and \(X,Y,U\) are schemes over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), so all the cited results stated for a prime power \(q\) and varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) will be applied with \(q\) replaced by \(q^m\) and \(\sigma\) replaced by \(\sigma_m\); this is legitimate because the statements are purely in terms of the prime power and the corresponding Frobenius.

**Step 1 (finiteness of the relevant spaces).** Since \(X\) is proper over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (applied with \(q\) replaced by \(q^m\) and with \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) carrying its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) shows that \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(n\). The same applies to \(Y\), which is smooth projective (hence proper) of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). In particular \(P^d\subseteq H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional.

Moreover, by lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_ordinary_gysin_sequence_open_complement (applied with \(q\) replaced by \(q^m\)) there is an exact sequence
\[
H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-1)\to H^{d+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
All terms other than \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) are finite-dimensional by the previous paragraph (Tate twists do not change the dimension), hence \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional as well. Here \(\partial\) is the connecting homomorphism of the Gysin sequence of \((X,Y)\).

**Step 2 (invertibility of \(F\)).** By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied with \(q\) replaced by \(q^m\) to the schemes \(X\), \(Y\), \(U\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)), the map \(F\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\). In particular \(F\) is an invertible operator on the finite-dimensional space \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

**Step 3 (the key identification).** We apply lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_as_affine_kernel. Its hypotheses are exactly the hypotheses of the present lemma: \(q=p^a\) is a prime power, \(\ell\neq p\), \(m\ge1\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\); \(X\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\); \(Y\subset X\) is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\); a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) has been fixed, identifying Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is the cycle class of \(Y\), \(L\) is cup product with \(\xi\), and \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\); and \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\). The conclusion of that lemma is that \(j^*\) restricts to an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules
\[
\alpha\;:\;P^d\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;K:=\ker\Bigl[\,\partial:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\,\Bigr],
\]
where \(\partial\) is the connecting homomorphism of the Gysin sequence of \((X,Y)\) (after the fixed identification of the Tate twist \((-1)\) with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)).

Being an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules, \(\alpha\) has the following two consequences, which we record explicitly:

(i) \(P^d\) is \(F\)-stable and \(K=\alpha(P^d)\) is an \(F\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear subspace of \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\);

(ii) \(\alpha\circ (F|_{P^d})=(F|_K)\circ\alpha\), i.e. \(\alpha\) intertwines the two \(F\)-actions.

(Equivalently, \(\partial\circ F=c\,F\circ\partial\) for some \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\) — the scalar arising from the Tate twist — so that \(\ker\partial\) is \(F\)-stable; but we do not need this, since (i) is part of the cited conclusion.)

**Step 4 (restriction to the stable subspace).** By hypothesis, \(F\) is semisimple on the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) (finiteness was checked in Step 1, invertibility in Step 2). Since \(K\) is an \(F\)-stable subspace by Step 3(i), lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 applies and yields that the restriction \(F|_K\) is a semisimple \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear operator on \(K\).

**Step 5 (transport to \(P^d\)).** We have a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(\alpha:P^d\to K\) with \(\alpha\circ(F|_{P^d})=(F|_K)\circ\alpha\) (Step 3(ii)). Both spaces are finite-dimensional (\(P^d\) by Step 1, \(K\subseteq H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) by Step 1). Both operators are invertible: \(F|_K\) is the restriction of the automorphism \(F\) of \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) to the \(F\)-stable subspace \(K\), hence injective on \(K\) and therefore bijective on the finite-dimensional space \(K\); and \(F|_{P^d}\) is conjugate to \(F|_K\) through \(\alpha\), hence is likewise bijective. Applying lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 to the pair \((P^d,F|_{P^d})\), \((K,F|_K)\) and the intertwining isomorphism \(\alpha\), we conclude that \(F|_{P^d}\) is semisimple if and only if \(F|_K\) is semisimple. By Step 4, \(F|_K\) is semisimple; hence \(F|_{P^d}\) is semisimple.

Therefore the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(F=(\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), acts semisimply on \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\), as claimed. No case was excluded: the argument covers all \(d\ge2\), all \(m\ge1\), and all primes \(\ell\neq p\); the hypothesis that \(Y\) is nonempty, effective, very ample, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) is used precisely to invoke lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_as_affine_kernel, and the hypothesis that \(L^{d-n}\) is an isomorphism for all \(0\le n\le d\) is used for the same purpose.

statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let ℓ be a prime different from char k, let X be a smooth projective connected variety of pure dimension 1 over k, let x ∈ X(k), and put U = X∖{x}. Then for every integer n ≥ 1 the Kummer sequence 0 → μ_{ℓ^n} → G_m → G_m → 0 on the étale site of U induces an isomorphism H^1_ét(U, μ_{ℓ^n}) ≅ Pic(U)[ℓ^n], these isomorphisms are compatible with the transition maps μ_{ℓ^{n+1}} → μ_{ℓ^n}, ζ ↦ ζ^ℓ, and with the maps Pic(U)[ℓ^{n+1}] → Pic(U)[ℓ^n], L ↦ L^{⊗ℓ}, and they induce an isomorphism lim_n H^1_ét(U, μ_{ℓ^n}) ≅ lim_n Pic(U)[ℓ^n].
proof:
Proof. Put μ_n=μ_{ℓ^n}. All cohomology below is étale cohomology. First, since ℓ is invertible on U, the Kummer sequence 0→μ_n→G_m→G_m→0 is exact on U_et. Indeed, for an étale V→U and a∈G_m(V)=O_V(V)^×, the algebra O_V[T]/(T^{ℓ^n}-a) is finite étale over V: its derivative ℓ^n T^{ℓ^n-1} is a unit because T is a unit in the quotient and ℓ is invertible. Over the corresponding cover V' the element T is an ℓ^n-th root of a. Hence the ℓ^n-power map G_m→G_m is an epimorphism of étale sheaves, and its kernel is μ_n.

We use the standard identification H^1_et(U,G_m)=Pic(U). Indeed, H^1_et(U,G_m) classifies étale G_m-torsors. A line bundle L gives the torsor L^×=Isom(O_U,L), and a G_m-torsor T gives the line bundle T×^{G_m}A^1; these constructions are inverse because both are étale-locally trivial. Under this identification the endomorphism [m]:G_m→G_m, t↦t^m, sends a torsor with transition functions g_{ij} to the one with transition functions g_{ij}^m; hence it sends a line bundle L to L^{⊗m}.

Next, H^0_et(U,G_m)=Γ(U,O_U)^×=k^×. Let f be a unit on U. Since U is a nonempty dense open subset of the integral curve X, f is a rational function on X. It has neither zeros nor poles on U, so its divisor on X is supported at x; thus div(f)=m[x] for some integer m. We claim deg div(f)=0. If f is constant this is clear. Otherwise f defines a finite morphism φ:X→P^1, and div(f)=φ^*((0)-(∞)); hence deg div(f)=deg(φ)·deg((0)-(∞))=0. Therefore m=0. Thus div(f)=0, so f extends to a nowhere-zero regular function on X. Since X is connected and projective, O_X(X)=k: a nonconstant global function would give a morphism X→A^1 whose image is a proper connected closed subset of A^1, hence a point. Therefore f∈k^×. Conversely every element of k^× is a unit on U. Thus H^0_et(U,G_m)=k^×.

Since k is algebraically closed and ℓ≠char k, every a∈k^× has an ℓ^n-th root in k^×; hence multiplication by ℓ^n on H^0_et(U,G_m) is surjective.

Consider the long exact cohomology sequence
0→H^0(U,μ_n)→H^0(U,G_m) --ℓ^n→ H^0(U,G_m) --δ_n→ H^1(U,μ_n) --α_n→ H^1(U,G_m) --ℓ^n→ H^1(U,G_m)→...
Since the map ℓ^n on H^0(U,G_m) is surjective, δ_n=0. Hence α_n is injective and its image is ker(ℓ^n:H^1(U,G_m)→H^1(U,G_m)). Under H^1(U,G_m)=Pic(U) and the identification of [ℓ^n] with L↦L^{⊗ℓ^n}, this kernel is Pic(U)[ℓ^n]. Thus α_n induces an isomorphism β_n:H^1(U,μ_n)≅Pic(U)[ℓ^n].

Now let θ_n:μ_{n+1}→μ_n, ζ↦ζ^ℓ, and let m_1:G_m→G_m, t↦t^ℓ. The diagram
0→μ_{n+1}→G_m --ℓ^{n+1}→ G_m→0
   ↓θ_n       ↓m_1              ↓id
0→μ_n→G_m --ℓ^n→ G_m→0
commutes: on the left, m_1(ζ)=ζ^ℓ=θ_n(ζ) for ζ∈μ_{n+1}; on the right, m_n(m_1(t))=t^{ℓ^{n+1}}=m_{n+1}(t). Naturality of the long exact sequence gives α_n∘θ_{n,*}=(m_1)_*∘α_{n+1}. Under H^1(U,G_m)=Pic(U), (m_1)_* is L↦L^{⊗ℓ}. Therefore for c∈H^1(U,μ_{n+1}),
β_n(θ_{n,*}c)=β_{n+1}(c)^{⊗ℓ}.
This is precisely the required compatibility with ζ↦ζ^ℓ and L↦L^{⊗ℓ}.

Thus the β_n form an isomorphism between the inverse systems (H^1(U,μ_n), θ_{n,*}) and (Pic(U)[ℓ^n], ⊗ℓ). Passing to inverse limits, with the left transition maps induced by θ_n and the right transition maps by L↦L^{⊗ℓ}, gives a canonical isomorphism
lim_n H^1_et(U,μ_{ℓ^n}) ≅ lim_n Pic(U)[ℓ^n].
Explicitly, a compatible sequence (c_n) maps to (β_n(c_n)); conversely a compatible sequence (L_n) gives c_n=β_n^{-1}(L_n), and compatibility follows from β_n(θ_{n,*}c_{n+1})=β_{n+1}(c_{n+1})^{⊗ℓ}=L_{n+1}^{⊗ℓ}=L_n. This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, let m≥1, put k equal to the algebraic closure of F_q, let d≥2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix an identification Q_ℓ(1)≅Q_ℓ, let ξ∈H^2_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) be the cycle class of a very ample divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let L be cup product with ξ. Suppose that L^{d−n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{2d−n}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0≤n≤d. Put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)). Then H^d_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)=P^d⊕L(H^{d−2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)) as Q_ℓ[F]-modules, where F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^{q^m}; in particular P^d is F-stable and the projection onto P^d along L(H^{d−2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)) is F-equivariant.
proof:
Write Q = q^m and H^n = H^n_et(X_k, Q_l). Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable with Q in place of its q. Its hypotheses hold: X is smooth projective of pure dimension d over F_Q, the given very ample F_Q-divisor has class xi, L is cup product with xi, and F = (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(u)=u^Q, is exactly the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. The lemma gives
   (star)  F o L = Q . L o F  on every H^n, and ker(L^{d-n+1}: H^n -> H^{2d-n+2}) is stable under F and F^{-1} for 0 <= n <= d.
Since l != p, Q = p^{am} is nonzero in Q_l, so (star) is equivalent to L o F = Q^{-1} F o L.

1. Injectivity of L: H^{d-2} -> H^d. As d >= 2, n = d-2 lies in [0,d], so the hypothesis says L^{d-(d-2)} = L^2 : H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2} is an isomorphism. If z in H^{d-2} has Lz = 0 in H^d, then L^2 z = 0, hence z = 0.

2. Sum. Let x in H^d. By surjectivity of L^2 : H^{d-2} -> H^{d+2} there is y in H^{d-2} with L^2 y = Lx. Then L(x - Ly) = Lx - L^2 y = 0, so x - Ly lies in ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}) = P^d. Thus H^d = P^d + L(H^{d-2}).

3. Directness. If z in H^{d-2} and Lz in P^d, then L^2 z = 0, so z = 0 by step 1 and Lz = 0. Hence H^d = P^d (+) L(H^{d-2}) as Q_l-vector spaces.

4. F-stability of the summands. For n = d the kernel in (star) is ker(L^{1}: H^d -> H^{2d-d+2} = H^{d+2}) = P^d, so P^d is F-stable (indeed F^{+-1}-stable); concretely, p in P^d gives L(Fp) = Q^{-1}F(Lp) = 0. And F(Lz) = Q L(Fz) in L(H^{d-2}) for z in H^{d-2}.

5. Conclusion. The addition map P^d (+) L(H^{d-2}) -> H^d is a Q_l-linear isomorphism by 2-3, and it is F-equivariant when F acts componentwise on the source, by 4; that is, H^d = P^d (+) L(H^{d-2}) as Q_l[F]-modules. Finally, for the projection pi onto P^d along L(H^{d-2}): writing x = p + Lz uniquely with p in P^d, one has Fx = Fp + F(Lz) with Fp in P^d and F(Lz) in L(H^{d-2}), so pi(Fx) = Fp = F(pi x); pi is F-equivariant. QED

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, let m≥1, let k be the algebraic closure of F_q, and let d≥2. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, and let Y⊂X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m} that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d−1. Fix an identification Q_ℓ(1)≅Q_ℓ. Let ξ∈H^2_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) be the cycle class of Y, let L_X be cup product with ξ, let i:Y→X be the closed immersion, put ξ_Y=i^*ξ, and let L_Y be cup product with ξ_Y. Then L_X^2:H^{d−2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism if and only if L_Y:H^{d−2}_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ)→H^d_et(Y_k,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism.
proof:
Proof. Throughout write H^n(X) := H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^n(Y) := H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Put q' := q^m = p^{am}; then \mathbb F_{q^m} = \mathbb F_{q'} and \overline{\mathbb F}_{q'} = \overline{\mathbb F}_q = k. The fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell corresponds to a nonzero element u \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1) (the preimage of 1); as in lemma_439 this identifies \mathbb Q_\ell(n) with \mathbb Q_\ell for every n \in \mathbb Z by u^n \mapsto 1. We use this same identification throughout, both for the cycle classes \xi, \xi_Y and for the traces.

0. Base-change facts. Since Y is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor on X defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, it is in particular a nonempty effective Cartier divisor. Since Y is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the base change Y_k is a nonempty smooth connected closed subscheme of X_k of pure dimension d-1. Moreover Y_k \subsetneq X_k, because dim Y_k = d-1 < d = dim X_k. The base change X_k is smooth projective and connected of pure dimension d over k (X is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^m}, so X_k is connected), and char k = p \neq \ell. Also Y is very ample, hence ample.

1. Weak Lefschetz: the restriction map \varphi := i^* is an isomorphism. Apply lemma_420 to the algebraically closed field k, the integer d \ge 2, the k-varieties X_k and Y_k, and the degree m := d-2. All hypotheses are satisfied: X_k is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d \ge 2 over k; Y_k \subsetneq X_k is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor which is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k. Since d \ge 2, we have d-2 < d-1, so lemma_420 yields that
\varphi := i^* : H^{d-2}(X) \longrightarrow H^{d-2}(Y)
is an isomorphism.

2. The degree-d Gysin map \psi is an isomorphism. Apply lemma_439 with q replaced by q' = q^m (so that the field called \mathbb F_q in its statement is our \mathbb F_{q^m}), with the same X, Y, d, \ell, and with the above nonzero u \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1). It provides, for every n \ge 0, the Gysin homomorphism i_! : H^n(Y) \to H^{n+2}(X), characterised by
(2.1)  tr_X(i_! a \cup b) = tr_Y(a \cup i^* b)   for all a \in H^n(Y), b \in H^{2d-2-n}(X),
where tr_X, tr_Y are the Poincare duality traces composed with the identification \mathbb Q_\ell(\dim) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell given by u^{\dim} \mapsto 1; and it also gives
(2.2)  i_!(i^* z) = z \cup \xi   for every n \ge 0 and every z \in H^n(X).
Let \psi := i_!^{(d)} : H^d(Y) \to H^{d+2}(X) be the degree-d Gysin map. Taking n = d in (2.1) gives
(2.3)  tr_X(\psi(a) \cup b) = tr_Y(a \cup \varphi(b))   for all a \in H^d(Y), b \in H^{d-2}(X).
We prove that \psi is an isomorphism.

(P1) The trace pairings are perfect. For Z \in \{X,Y\} let tr^{77}_Z be the normalized trace of lemma_77(a) applied to Z over \mathbb F_{q^m} (so Z = X of pure dimension d, or Z = Y of pure dimension d-1), composed with the identification \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim Z) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell. By lemma_77(a), tr^{77}_Z : H^{2\dim Z}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim Z) is an isomorphism; hence H^{2\dim Z}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space and tr^{77}_Z, viewed as a \mathbb Q_\ell-valued functional, is nonzero. The trace tr_Z of lemma_439 is the Poincare duality trace H^{2\dim Z}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim Z) composed with the identification \mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim Z) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell; the Poincare duality trace is by definition the canonical isomorphism furnished by Poincare duality, namely the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism exhibited in lemma_77(a). Hence tr_Z is also an isomorphism onto \mathbb Q_\ell, in particular nonzero. Two nonzero \mathbb Q_\ell-linear functionals on a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space differ by a nonzero scalar, so there is c_Z \in \mathbb Q_\ell^\times with
(2.4)  tr_Z = c_Z \cdot tr^{77}_Z.
By lemma_77(b) applied to Z = X (pure dimension d) with n = d+2 (legitimate since 0 \le d+2 \le 2d because d \ge 2), the pairing
H^{d+2}(X) \times H^{d-2}(X) \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),  (y,x) \mapsto tr^{77}_X(y \cup x),
is perfect; after the identification \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell and after multiplying by the nonzero scalar c_X (see (2.4)), the pairing
(2.5)  H^{d+2}(X) \times H^{d-2}(X) \to \mathbb Q_\ell,  (y,x) \mapsto tr_X(y \cup x),
is perfect. Similarly, lemma_77(b) applied to Z = Y (pure dimension d-1) with n = d (legitimate since 0 \le d \le 2(d-1) because d \ge 2) shows that
(2.6)  H^d(Y) \times H^{d-2}(Y) \to \mathbb Q_\ell,  (b,a) \mapsto tr_Y(b \cup a),
is a perfect pairing.

(P2) Adjoint isomorphisms. Define
\alpha : H^{d+2}(X) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{d-2}(X),\mathbb Q_\ell),   \alpha(y)(x) := tr_X(y \cup x),
\beta : H^d(Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{d-2}(Y),\mathbb Q_\ell),   \beta(b)(a) := tr_Y(b \cup a).
Perfectness of (2.5) means precisely that \alpha is an isomorphism: for a perfect pairing \langle-, -\rangle : V \times W \to \mathbb Q_\ell, the induced map V \to W^\vee, v \mapsto \langle v, -\rangle, is an isomorphism. Likewise, perfectness of (2.6) means precisely that \beta is an isomorphism.

(P3) \psi is the transpose of \varphi. Let \varphi^\vee : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{d-2}(Y),\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{d-2}(X),\mathbb Q_\ell) be the transpose of \varphi, i.e. (\varphi^\vee f)(x) = f(\varphi(x)). For a \in H^d(Y) and y \in H^{d-2}(X), using (2.3) with b = y, we compute
\alpha(\psi(a))(y) = tr_X(\psi(a) \cup y) = tr_Y(a \cup \varphi(y)) = \beta(a)(\varphi(y)) = (\varphi^\vee(\beta(a)))(y).
Every equality here is literal: the first and third are the definitions of \alpha and \beta, the second is exactly (2.3) with b = y, and the fourth is the definition of the transpose. Hence
(2.7)  \alpha \circ \psi = \varphi^\vee \circ \beta.

(P4) Conclusion of Step 2. By Step 1, \varphi is an isomorphism, hence so is \varphi^\vee, with inverse (\varphi^{-1})^\vee. By (P2), \alpha and \beta are isomorphisms. From (2.7), \psi = \alpha^{-1} \circ \varphi^\vee \circ \beta, a composite of isomorphisms; therefore
\psi : H^d(Y) \longrightarrow H^{d+2}(X) is an isomorphism.

3. Factorization of L_X^2. For x \in H^{d-2}(X) we compute
\psi(L_Y(\varphi(x))) = \psi(\varphi(x) \cup \xi_Y) = i_!(\varphi(x) \cup \xi_Y) = i_!(i^*x \cup i^*\xi) = i_!(i^*(x \cup \xi)) = (x \cup \xi) \cup \xi = x \cup \xi^2 = L_X^2(x).
Here: the first equality uses the definitions L_Y = (-) \cup \xi_Y and \xi_Y = i^*\xi; the second is the definition \psi = i_! in degree d; the third uses \varphi = i^* and \xi_Y = i^*\xi; the fourth uses that i^* is a ring homomorphism; the fifth is (2.2) with n = d and z = x \cup \xi \in H^d(X); the sixth is associativity of the cup product; and the last is the definition L_X = (-) \cup \xi. Thus
(3.1)  L_X^2 = \psi \circ L_Y \circ \varphi   as maps H^{d-2}(X) \to H^{d+2}(X).

4. The equivalence. By Steps 1 and 2, \varphi : H^{d-2}(X) \to H^{d-2}(Y) and \psi : H^d(Y) \to H^{d+2}(X) are isomorphisms.
- If L_X^2 is an isomorphism, then by (3.1) L_Y = \psi^{-1} \circ L_X^2 \circ \varphi^{-1} is a composite of isomorphisms, hence an isomorphism.
- If L_Y is an isomorphism, then by (3.1) L_X^2 = \psi \circ L_Y \circ \varphi is a composite of isomorphisms, hence an isomorphism.
Therefore L_X^2 : H^{d-2}(X) \to H^{d+2}(X) is an isomorphism if and only if L_Y : H^{d-2}(Y) \to H^d(Y) is an isomorphism. This proves the lemma. No semisimplicity, no Hard Lefschetz, and no injectivity of a Gysin map at degree d-1 is assumed or used; the only inputs are weak Lefschetz on X (lemma_420), the Gysin projection formula of lemma_439, and Poincare duality (lemma_77). \qed

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, let m≥1, put k equal to the algebraic closure of F_q, and let d≥2. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let B⊂X be a nonempty smooth closed subvariety of pure dimension d−2 defined over F_{q^m}, and let π:X'=Bl_B X→X be the blow-up of X along B. Let F_X', F_X, and F_B be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^{q^m}, of H^*_et(X'_k,Q_ℓ), H^*_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), and H^*_et(B_k,Q_ℓ), respectively. Then F_X' is semisimple on H^d_et(X'_k,Q_ℓ) if and only if F_X is semisimple on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) and F_B is semisimple on H^{d−2}_et(B_k,Q_ℓ).
proof:
Put Q = q^m. Then Q = p^{am} is a prime power, and since l != p, Q is nonzero in Q_l (indeed Q is a l-adic unit). The algebraic closure of F_Q is the same k, and the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius in the statement is exactly the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius.

Let V_X = H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) and V_B = H^{d-2}_et(B_k,Q_l). These are finite-dimensional Q_l-vector spaces, and F_X and F_B are invertible Q_l-linear operators. The blow-up X' = Bl_B X is smooth projective over F_Q, and because B is nonempty it is geometrically connected, so it satisfies the hypotheses of the blow-up cohomology formula.

Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_415 with the prime power Q in place of its q. For n=d it gives an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces
H^d_et(X'_k,Q_l) ≅ V_X ⊕ V_B(-1)
under which F_X' corresponds to F_X on the first summand and to Q times F_B on the second summand. To compare this with the untwisted group V_B appearing in the desired conclusion, choose a nonzero element tau of Q_l(-1). The map phi: V_B -> V_B(-1), v -> v ⊗ tau, is a Q_l-linear isomorphism, and the action described by lemma_415 says precisely that F_{V_B(-1)}(phi(v)) = phi(Q F_B(v)). Equivalently, after this identification, the blow-up formula is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules
H^d_et(X'_k,Q_l) ≅ (V_X, F_X) ⊕ (V_B, Q F_B).

By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, semisimplicity of an invertible operator is invariant under an isomorphism of the underlying vector spaces that intertwines the operators. Hence F_X' is semisimple on H^d_et(X'_k,Q_l) if and only if the direct-sum operator F_X ⊕ (Q F_B) is semisimple on V_X ⊕ V_B.

By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9, a direct-sum operator is semisimple if and only if each of its summand operators is semisimple. Thus F_X ⊕ (Q F_B) is semisimple if and only if F_X is semisimple on V_X and Q F_B is semisimple on V_B.

By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248, since Q is a nonzero scalar in Q_l, Q F_B is semisimple on V_B if and only if F_B is semisimple on V_B.

Combining the equivalences gives
F_X' is semisimple on H^d_et(X'_k,Q_l) if and only if F_X is semisimple on H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) and F_B is semisimple on H^{d-2}_et(B_k,Q_l).

The case d=2 is included: then V_B = H^0_et(B_k,Q_l), and the same argument applies verbatim. If a cohomology space under consideration is zero, the corresponding semisimplicity assertion is vacuous and the cited lemmas still apply.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, let m≥1, put k equal to the algebraic closure of F_q, and let d≥2. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, and let Y⊂X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m} that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d−1. Fix an identification Q_ℓ(1)≅Q_ℓ, let ξ∈H^2_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) be the cycle class of Y, let L be cup product with ξ, and put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)→H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ)). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^{q^m}. Suppose that F is semisimple on H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), and that there exist finitely many classes η_1,...,η_r∈H^2_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) fixed by F such that the common kernel of the maps x↦η_j∪x from P^d to H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ℓ), for j=1,...,r, is zero. Then F is semisimple on P^d.
proof:
Write Q := q^m = p^{am}, a prime power, so that X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_Q and Y is an F_Q-rational very ample divisor with class xi. Write H^n := H^n_et(X_k, Q_l).

(1) Finite dimensionality and invertibility. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (with Q in place of its q, to the proper F_Q-scheme X and the constant sheaf Q_l with its natural Frobenius structure) each H^n is finite-dimensional over Q_l and carries a canonical Q_l-linear arithmetic Frobenius automorphism; eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a identifies this operator with F = (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c) = c^Q, and gives that it is invertible with inverse the geometric Frobenius.

(2) Edge case r = 0. The common kernel of an empty family of maps is all of P^d, so the hypothesis forces P^d = 0, and the zero operator on the zero space is semisimple. Henceforth assume r >= 1.

(3) F-stability of P^d. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable to X over F_Q with the very ample F_Q-divisor Y, xi = cl(Y) and L = cup xi (d >= 2 so 0 <= d <= d is allowed): with m := d its kernel is ker(L^{d-d+1} = L : H^d -> H^{d+2}) = P^d, and the lemma states this space is stable under F and under F^{-1} (the relation F o L = Q . L o F with Q != 0 is what gives stability). Thus T := F|_{P^d} is a well-defined element of GL_{Q_l}(P^d), P^d being finite-dimensional by (1).

(4) The embedding into a semisimple space. Set V := (H^{d+2})^r, T_V := F^{oplus r} in GL(V), and Phi : P^d -> V, Phi(x) := (eta_1 cup x, ..., eta_r cup x). Cup product is Q_l-bilinear, so Phi is Q_l-linear; it is injective because ker Phi = cap_{j=1}^r {x in P^d : eta_j cup x = 0} = 0 by hypothesis.

(5) T_V is semisimple: F is semisimple on H^{d+2} by assumption and invertible by (1), so eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 applied to the r copies of H^{d+2} gives that T_V = direct sum of r copies of a semisimple invertible operator is semisimple on the finite-dimensional space V.

(6) Equivariance. For x in P^d and 1 <= j <= r, using eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_220 (F(a cup b) = Fa cup Fb on H^*, with no scalar factor; the scalar Q in step (3) arose only from F acting on xi) and F(eta_j) = eta_j:
    Phi(Fx)_j = eta_j cup Fx = F(eta_j) cup F(x) = F(eta_j cup x) = T_V(Phi(x))_j,
so Phi o T = T_V o Phi. Consequently W := im Phi is T_V-stable, and Phi induces a T-equivariant Q_l-linear isomorphism P^d ~-> W.

(7) Restriction to W. W is finite-dimensional (a subspace of V), and T_V|_W lies in GL(W) since W is T_V-stable and T_V is injective on the finite-dimensional W. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515, the restriction of the semisimple operator T_V to the stable subspace W is semisimple.

(8) Conclusion. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 to the isomorphism Phi : P^d ~-> W with T_V = F|_{P^d} and T_W = T_V|_W (both invertible, both spaces finite-dimensional by (1)): T = F|_{P^d} is semisimple.

This is exactly the required statement: the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on P^d = ker(L : H^d_et(X_k, Q_l) -> H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_l)).

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(f:V\to C\) be a smooth proper morphism of relative dimension \(n\ge1\) with geometrically connected fibres, where \(C\) is a smooth affine geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). For each \(r\ge0\) write \(\mathcal H^r=R^rf_{k*}\mathbb Q_\ell\) for the lisse sheaf on \(C_k\), and let \(F\) denote the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and on the cohomology of \(C_k\) with coefficients in the \(\mathcal H^r\). Then the Leray edge maps give a short exact sequence of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules \[0\to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^{n-1})\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^{n})\to 0.\]
proof:
Write g = f_k : V_k -> C_k for the base change of f to k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, and put \mathcal H^r = R^r g_* \mathbb Q_\ell.

Step 1 (the base). Since C is an affine scheme of finite type over \mathbb F_{q^m} of Krull dimension 1, its base change C_k is again affine of finite type over the algebraically closed field k, of Krull dimension 1 (affineness and finite type are preserved by base change, and a smooth curve has dimension 1, which is preserved by the flat base change Spec k -> Spec \mathbb F_{q^m}).

Step 2 (the sheaves and the spectral sequence). The morphism f is smooth and proper, so by proper base change for the geometric points of C_k the groups H^q((V_k)_{\bar c}, \mathbb Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional and, by the smooth base change theorem, R^q g_* \mathbb Z/\ell^m is lisse of finite rank for every m; passing to the inverse system, \mathcal H^q = R^q g_* \mathbb Q_\ell is a lisse, hence constructible, \mathbb Q_\ell-sheaf on C_k (this is the definition of the sheaf appearing in the statement). The Leray spectral sequence for g and the constant complex \mathbb Q_\ell (Milne, Étale Cohomology III.2.20; SGA 4\frac12, Th. 1.1) is a first-quadrant spectral sequence of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
  E_2^{p,q} = H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k, \mathcal H^q)  =>  H^{p+q}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k, \mathbb Q_\ell),
converging to the cohomology of the total space, with abutment filtration F^\bullet.

Step 3 (vanishing of the base cohomology above degree 1). Fix r \ge 0 and apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_288 with U = C_k (so its integer n is 1), with the prime \ell as in the statement (\ell \neq p = char k), and with K = \mathcal H^r[0]. This K lies in D^b_c(C_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}, \mathbb Q_\ell) by Step 2 and satisfies \mathcal H^q(K) = 0 for q > 0 since it is concentrated in degree 0. The lemma gives H^q(R\Gamma(C_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}, \mathcal H^r[0])) = 0 for q > 1, i.e.
  H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k, \mathcal H^r) = 0 for all p > 1.
Hence E_2^{p,q} = 0 whenever p \ge 2.

Step 4 (degeneration). The r-th differential of the Leray spectral sequence has bidegree (r, 1-r) for r \ge 2, i.e. d_r : E_r^{p,q} -> E_r^{p+r, q-r+1}. For p = 0 or p = 1 the target has first index p+r \ge 2 and is therefore 0; and for p \ge 2 the source is already 0, so no non-zero term can receive a differential from a column p \ge 2 either. Thus all differentials are zero from E_2 onwards: the spectral sequence degenerates at E_2 and E_2^{p,q} = E_\infty^{p,q} for all p,q.

Step 5 (the five-term identification in total degree n). The abutment filtration on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite, decreasing, separated and exhaustive, with graded pieces gr_F^p H^n = E_\infty^{p,\,n-p}. Since n \ge 1 and E_\infty^{p,q} = 0 for p \ge 2 (Step 3-4) and for p < 0 (first quadrant), the only possibly non-zero pieces with p+q = n are E_\infty^{0,n} = H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^n) and E_\infty^{1,n-1} = H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^{n-1}). Therefore
  0 = F^2 H^n \subseteq F^1 H^n \subseteq F^0 H^n = H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
with F^1H^n = gr_F^1 H^n \cong E_\infty^{1,n-1} = H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^{n-1}) and H^n/F^1H^n = gr_F^0 H^n \cong E_\infty^{0,n} = H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^n). By construction these two isomorphisms are the Leray edge maps: the surjection H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \twoheadrightarrow H^0(C_k,\mathcal H^n) is the edge homomorphism obtained by restricting a class to the generic behaviour of the fibration (the composition H^n \to E_\infty^{0,n} \hookrightarrow E_2^{0,n}), and the injection H^1(C_k,\mathcal H^{n-1}) \hookrightarrow H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is the other edge map, whose image is exactly the kernel of the first. Splicing these two exact pieces gives the short exact sequence
  0 \to H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^{n-1}) \longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathcal H^n) \to 0.

Step 6 (Frobenius linearity). Let \sigma(c) = c^{q^m} and let F_C = (id_{C_k} \times Spec\sigma)^* and F_V = (id_{V_k}\times Spec\sigma)^*; these satisfy g \circ F_V = F_C \circ g because f is defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}. Functoriality of proper/smooth base change identifies the pullback of \mathcal H^r along F_C with R^r(F_C)_* g_* \mathbb Q_\ell \cong R^r (g\circ F_V)_* \mathbb Q_\ell \cong F_V^* \mathcal H^r, so F induces a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \mathcal H^r \xrightarrow{\sim} F_C^* \mathcal H^r, hence isomorphisms on each E_2^{p,q} = H^p(C_k,\mathcal H^q). The Leray spectral sequence is natural in the morphism g, so these isomorphisms assemble into an automorphism of the spectral sequence which on the abutment is F_V (SGA 4\frac12, Th. 1.1; Milne III.2.20). Naturality also identifies the edge maps and the filtration pieces with F-stable subspaces: F(F^p H^n) = F^p H^n. Consequently the two outer terms and the middle term in the sequence of Step 5 are \mathbb Q_\ell[F]-modules and the two displayed maps are F-equivariant, so the sequence is a short exact sequence of \mathbb Q_\ell[F]-modules.

(Remark: the hypothesis of geometrically connected fibres is not used above; it is part of the ambient setup and only affects the identification of \mathcal H^0 with the constant sheaf.) This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(K\) be a field, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\). Let \(r\ge1\), and for \(j=1,\dots,r\) let \(W_j\) be a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, let \(T_j\in\operatorname{GL}_K(W_j)\) be semisimple, and let \(\varphi_j:W_j\to V\) be a \(K\)-linear map satisfying \(T\circ\varphi_j=\varphi_j\circ T_j\). If \(V=\varphi_1(W_1)+\cdots+\varphi_r(W_r)\), then \(T\) is semisimple on \(V\).
proof:
Let \bar K be an algebraic closure of K. We use the standard characterization of semisimple operators over an arbitrary field: for a finite-dimensional K-vector space U and S\in GL_K(U), S is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial \mu_S\in K[t] is a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials; equivalently, S\otimes_K id_{\bar K} is diagonalizable over \bar K. For completeness, if S is diagonalizable over \bar K then \mu_{S\otimes id_{\bar K}}=\prod_{\lambda}(t-\lambda) with distinct \lambda, so \mu_S cannot contain a repeated or inseparable irreducible factor; conversely, if \mu_S=\prod_i f_i with the f_i distinct separable irreducibles, then over \bar K it is \prod_{\lambda}(t-\lambda) with distinct \lambda, and the Lagrange idempotents e_\lambda(t)=\prod_{\mu\ne\lambda}(t-\mu)/(\lambda-\mu) give a direct-sum decomposition of U\otimes_K\bar K into eigenspaces. The only consequences of this criterion used below are that monic divisors and finite least common multiples of products of distinct separable irreducible polynomials again have that form, which is immediate from unique factorization in K[t].

If V=0, then T is semisimple, so assume V\neq 0. For each j put U_j=\varphi_j(W_j). Discard any j for which U_j=0. For the remaining indices, U_j is a nonzero finite-dimensional K-subspace.

First, U_j is T-stable: for u=\varphi_j(w)\in U_j,
T(u)=T\varphi_j(w)=\varphi_j(T_j w)\in U_j.
Since T is invertible and U_j is finite-dimensional, T(U_j)=U_j, so S_j:=T|_{U_j} is an element of GL_K(U_j).

Next, N_j:=\ker\varphi_j is T_j-stable: if w\in N_j, then
\varphi_j(T_j w)=T\varphi_j(w)=T(0)=0.
Thus T_j induces an automorphism \bar T_j of W_j/N_j. (Indeed T_j(N_j)=N_j by the same dimension argument, so T_j^{-1} also preserves N_j.) The map \varphi_j induces a K-linear isomorphism
\tilde\varphi_j: W_j/N_j \xrightarrow{\sim} U_j,\quad \tilde\varphi_j(w+N_j)=\varphi_j(w),
and this isomorphism intertwines the two operators:
\tilde\varphi_j\circ\bar T_j=S_j\circ\tilde\varphi_j.
Consequently S_j and \bar T_j have the same minimal polynomial.

Because \mu_{T_j}(T_j)=0, the polynomial \mu_{T_j} also annihilates the induced operator \bar T_j on the quotient: for every w\in W_j,
\mu_{T_j}(\bar T_j)(w+N_j)=\mu_{T_j}(T_j)w+N_j=0+N_j.
Hence \mu_{\bar T_j} divides \mu_{T_j}. By the semisimplicity of T_j, \mu_{T_j} is a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials. By the divisor property, \mu_{\bar T_j} is again a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials. Therefore \mu_{S_j}=\mu_{\bar T_j} has the same form, and S_j=T|_{U_j} is semisimple.

Now V=\sum_j U_j. For each remaining j let \mu_j:=\mu_{S_j}. Each \mu_j is a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials. Let
M=\operatorname{lcm}(\mu_j).
By the least-common-multiple property, M is again a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials. Since \mu_j divides M, we have M(S_j)=0, i.e. M(T) kills U_j.
