Because V is the sum of the U_j, M(T) kills all of V. Therefore the minimal polynomial \mu_T of T divides M (the minimal polynomial divides every polynomial annihilating T). By the divisor property, \mu_T is again a product of distinct separable irreducible polynomials. By the characterization recalled at the beginning, T is semisimple.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, let N ≥ 0, and let H = ⊕_{n ≥ 0} H^n be a finite-dimensional graded-commutative and graded-cocommutative Hopf algebra over k with H^0 = k and comultiplication Δ. Suppose dim_k H^1 = N, H^n = 0 for every n > N, and dim_k H^N = 1. Then the elements x ∈ H satisfying Δ(x) = x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x are exactly H^1.
proof:
Write $P=\{x\in H:\Delta(x)=x\otimes 1+1\otimes x\}$ for the primitive subspace, and let $\varepsilon:H\to k$ be the counit. Since $\varepsilon$ is a graded algebra map of degree $0$ and $k$ is concentrated in degree $0$, $\varepsilon(H^n)=0$ for all $n\ge1$, and $\varepsilon(1)=1$.

(1) $P$ is graded, and $P\cap H^0=0$. $\Delta$ is homogeneous of degree $0$, so $\Delta(H^n)\subset\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p\otimes H^q$. If $z=\sum_n z_n\in P$ ($z_n$ homogeneous of degree $n$), comparing the bidegree $(n,0)$ components of $\Delta(z)=z\otimes1+1\otimes z$ gives $\Delta(z_n)_{(n,0)}=z_n\otimes1$, comparing $(0,n)$ gives $\Delta(z_n)_{(0,n)}=1\otimes z_n$, and comparing $(p,q)$ with $p,q>0$ gives $\Delta(z_n)_{(p,q)}=0$ (only $z_n$ contributes to total degree $n$). Hence each $z_n\in P$. For $z=\lambda\cdot1\in H^0$: $\Delta(\lambda\cdot1)=\lambda\cdot1\otimes1$ while $\lambda\cdot1\otimes1+1\otimes\lambda\cdot1=2\lambda\cdot1\otimes1$, so $\lambda=2\lambda$ and $\lambda=0$ as $\mathrm{char}\,k=0$.

(2) $H^1\subset P$. For $x\in H^1$, $\Delta(x)\in(H\otimes H)^1=k\cdot1\otimes H^1\oplus H^1\otimes k\cdot1$, so $\Delta(x)=1\otimes u+v\otimes1$ with $u,v\in H^1$. Applying $\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}$ and using $\varepsilon(v)=0$ gives $x=u$; applying $\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon$ gives $x=v$. Thus $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$.

(3) The exterior subalgebra. Graded commutativity gives $a^2=-a^2$ for $a\in H^1$, hence $a^2=0$ ($\mathrm{char}\,k=0$). So the multiplication of $H$ induces a graded algebra map $\psi:\bigwedge^*V\to H$, $V:=H^1$ (concentrated in degree $1$), which in degree $n$ is the map $\bigwedge^n H^1\to H^n$ induced by multiplication; by Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_exterior_subalgebra_injects it is injective for every $n$. Put $B=\mathrm{im}\,\psi$, $B^n=\psi(\bigwedge^n V)$; then $B^n\subset H^n$, $B^0=k\cdot1$, $\dim_k B^n=\dim_k\bigwedge^n V=\binom{N}{n}$, and $B=0$ for $n>N$.

Endow $\bigwedge^*V$ with the Hopf structure for which $V$ is primitive ($\Delta$ the algebra map into the Koszul tensor product, $\varepsilon$ the projection onto $\bigwedge^0V=k$). Since every element of $V=H^1$ is primitive by (2) and $\Delta$ is an algebra map, the two algebra maps $\Delta\circ\psi$ and $(\psi\otimes\psi)\circ\Delta$ of $\bigwedge^*V$ into $H\otimes H$ agree on the generators $V$, hence everywhere. So $\psi$ is a Hopf map, $\Delta(B)\subset B\otimes B$, and $\psi:\bigwedge^*V\xrightarrow{\sim}B$ is an isomorphism of graded Hopf algebras.

(4) Primitives of $\bigwedge^*V$, computed directly. Fix a basis $e_1,\dots,e_N$ of $V$; for $I=\{i_1<\dots<i_d\}$ write $e_I=e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_d}$. Expanding $\Delta(e_I)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(e_{i_j}\otimes1+1\otimes e_{i_j})$ with the Koszul rule $(u\otimes v)(a\otimes b)=(-1)^{\deg v\deg a}ua\otimes vb$, the bidegree $(1,d-1)$ component is
$\Phi(e_I):=\Delta(e_I)_{(1,d-1)}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\pm\, e_{i_j}\otimes e_{I\setminus\{i_j\}}$,
with each coefficient $\pm1$ (this sign bookkeeping is also verified by explicit exact-integer computation for $N\le6$). The linear map $\Phi:\bigwedge^dV\to V\otimes\bigwedge^{d-1}V$, $w\mapsto\Delta(w)_{(1,d-1)}$, is injective for $d\ge2$: if $I\ne I'$ the basis tensors occurring in $\Phi(e_I)$ and $\Phi(e_{I'})$ are disjoint, since $e_{i}\otimes e_{I\setminus\{i\}}=e_{i'}\otimes e_{I'\setminus\{i'\}}$ forces $i=i'$ and then $I=I'$; hence the vectors $\Phi(e_I)$, $|I|=d$, have pairwise disjoint support in a basis and are nonzero, so they are linearly independent.

Now let $w\in\bigwedge^dV$ be primitive. If $d\ge2$, then $w\otimes1+1\otimes w$ has bidegrees $(d,0)$ and $(0,d)$ only, so $0=\Delta(w)_{(1,d-1)}=\Phi(w)$, whence $w=0$ by injectivity. If $d=0$, $w$ is a scalar multiple of $1$, and $P\cap\bigwedge^0V=0$ by the same $\lambda=2\lambda$ argument as in (1). Degree $1$ is primitive by definition. Thus $P(\bigwedge^*V)=V$, and transporting along the Hopf isomorphism $\psi$, $P(B)=B^1=H^1$. Finally, if $b\in B\cap P(H)$ then $\Delta_H(b)=b\otimes1+1\otimes b\in B\otimes B$; as $B$ is a graded $k$-subspace of $H$ over a field it is a direct summand, so $B\otimes B\to H\otimes H$ is injective and $b$ is primitive in $B$. Hence $P(H)\cap B=P(B)=H^1$.

(5) No primitives in degrees $\ge2$. Let $z\in P\cap H^d$ with $d\ge2$; if $d>N$ then $H^d=0$ by hypothesis, so assume $2\le d\le N$ (in particular $N\ge2$). By (4), $z\notin B=\bigoplus_nB^n$ (as $P\cap B=H^1\subset H^1$ and $z$ is homogeneous of degree $d\ge2$). Let $\pi:H\to H/B$ be the quotient map; then $\pi(z)\ne0$. Choose $0\ne x\in B^N$: it exists and is nonzero because $\dim_kB^N=\dim_k\bigwedge^NV=\binom NN=1$ and $\psi$ is injective in degree $N$; also $x\in H^N$.

Since $\deg(zx)=d+N>N$ and $H^{n}=0$ for $n>N$, $zx=0$, so $0=\Delta(zx)=\Delta(z)\Delta(x)=(z\otimes1+1\otimes z)\Delta(x)$. As $B$ is a Hopf subalgebra and $x\in B^N$, $\Delta(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N}w_i$ with $w_i\in B^i\otimes B^{N-i}$. Applying $\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}$ (which kills $w_i$ for $i\ge1$, since $\varepsilon(B^i)=0$ there) gives $w_0=1\otimes x$; applying $\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon$ gives $w_N=x\otimes1$. For $1\le i\le N-1$ write $w_i=\sum_j a_{ij}\otimes b_{ij}$ with $a_{ij}\in B^{i}$, $b_{ij}\in B^{N-i}$. Using the Koszul rule,
$0=\big(z\otimes x+\textstyle\sum_{i,j}z a_{ij}\otimes b_{ij}\big)+\big((-1)^{dN}x\otimes z+\textstyle\sum_{i,j}(-1)^{id}a_{ij}\otimes z b_{ij}\big).$
Apply $\pi\otimes\mathrm{id}:H\otimes H\to(H/B)\otimes H$ and then project onto the summand $(H/B)\otimes H^N$ (legal since $H=\bigoplus_qH^q$). In the first parenthesis, $\pi(1)=\pi(x)=0$ and $b_{ij}$ has degree $N-i$, so only $i=0$ survives, contributing $\pi(z)\otimes x$. In the second, $\pi(x)=0$ kills $(-1)^{dN}\pi(x)\otimes z$, and $z b_{ij}$ has degree $d+N-i$, which equals $N$ only for $i=d$; for that $i$ each $a_{dj}\in B^d$ satisfies $\pi(a_{dj})=0$. Hence the projection is exactly $\pi(z)\otimes x=0$, impossible since $\pi(z)\ne0$, $x\ne0$, and a tensor of two nonzero vectors over a field is nonzero. Thus $P\cap H^d=0$ for all $d\ge2$.

(6) Conclusion. By (1) every primitive is a sum of homogeneous primitives; degrees $0$ (step 1) and $\ge2$ (step 5) contribute nothing, and degree $1$ is exactly $H^1$ by (2). Hence $P=H^1$. (If $N=0$ then $H=H^0=k\cdot1$ and step 1 gives $P=0=H^1$; if $N=1$ then $H^d=0$ for $d\ge2$ and step 5 is vacuous; both are consistent with the argument above.)

statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(k\), let \(Y\subsetneq X\) be a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor that is smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(k\), and put \(U=X\setminus Y\). For every integer \(a\), the cup-product pairing \[ H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2d-a}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell) \] induces a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \[ H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-a}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell),H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr). \]
proof:
We fix the notation of the statement: $k$ is algebraically closed, $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)$ is prime, $X$ is smooth projective connected of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ over $k$, $Y\subsetneq X$ is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor smooth of pure dimension $d-1$, and $U=X\setminus Y$ with its open subscheme structure. For an integer $n$ we abbreviate
\[
V_n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad W_n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad T:=H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
The cup product $V_a\times W_{2d-a}\to T$, $(x,y)\mapsto x\cup y$, is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear (bilinearity of the pairings $R\Gamma_c(-)\times R\Gamma(-)\to R\Gamma_c(-)$ on cohomology of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$), hence for each $x\in V_a$ the map $y\mapsto x\cup y$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear element of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W_{2d-a},T)$, and the assignment
\[
\Psi_a:V_a\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W_{2d-a},T),\qquad \Psi_a(x)(y)=x\cup y,
\]
is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear. This is precisely the map whose being an isomorphism the lemma asserts. We prove it is an isomorphism in four steps.

\textbf{Step 1: the geometric duality input.} By the proved lemma \texttt{Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_admissible_affine_poincare_duality}, whose hypotheses are exactly the hypotheses of the present lemma on $(k,\ell,X,Y,U)$, there exists a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{tr}:T=H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)
\]
such that for \emph{every} integer $j$ the pairing
\[
B_j:V_j\times W_{2d-j}\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad B_j(x,y):=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y),
\]
is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Applying this with $j=a$ we obtain: $V_a$ and $W_{2d-a}$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and $B_a$ is perfect, i.e. non-degenerate in each variable: $B_a(x,y)=0$ for all $y$ implies $x=0$, and $B_a(x,y)=0$ for all $x$ implies $y=0$. Note that $B_a$ is exactly the cup-product pairing followed by $\operatorname{tr}$.

\textbf{Step 2: an elementary linear-algebra fact.}
\emph{Claim.} Let $K$ be a field, let $L$ be a one-dimensional $K$-vector space, let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $K$-vector spaces, and let $B:V\times W\to L$ be a perfect $K$-bilinear pairing. Then
\[
\Phi_B:V\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_K(W,L),\qquad \Phi_B(v)(w)=B(v,w),
\]
is a $K$-linear isomorphism.
\emph{Proof of the claim.} $K$-linearity of $\Phi_B$ is immediate from bilinearity of $B$: $\Phi_B(\lambda v+\mu v')(w)=B(\lambda v+\mu v',w)=\lambda B(v,w)+\mu B(v',w)=(\lambda\Phi_B(v)+\mu\Phi_B(v'))(w)$ for all $w$. Choose a $K$-basis element $\lambda\in L$, i.e. the isomorphism $\lambda:K\xrightarrow{\sim}L$, $c\mapsto c\cdot\lambda_0$, where $\lambda_0$ is the chosen basis vector; put $B_0:=\lambda^{-1}\circ B:V\times W\to K$. Then $B_0$ is again perfect, and $\Phi_B=(\text{post-composition with }\lambda)\circ\Phi_{B_0}$; since post-composition with the isomorphism $\lambda:K\to L$ is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}_K(W,K)\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(W,L)$, it suffices to treat the case $L=K$, $B=B_0$.

Let $e_1,\dots,e_m$ be a basis of $V$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ a basis of $W$, and let $M=(\mu_{ij})\in\operatorname{Mat}_{m\times n}(K)$ with $\mu_{ij}=B(e_i,f_j)$. For $a=(a_1,\dots,a_m)$ and $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ one has $B(\sum_i a_ie_i,\sum_j b_jf_j)=a^{t}Mb$ (viewing $a,b$ as column vectors).

Non-degeneracy in the second variable says: if $x=\sum_i a_ie_i$ satisfies $B(x,f_j)=0$ for all $j$, then $x=0$. Now $B(x,f_j)=\sum_i a_i\mu_{ij}$, i.e. the row vector $a^{t}M$; so $a^{t}M=0\Rightarrow a=0$. Thus the transpose map $M^{t}:K^{m}\to K^{n}$, $a\mapsto M^{t}a=(a^{t}M)^{t}$, is injective, whence $\operatorname{rank}M=m$ and $m\le n$.

Non-degeneracy in the first variable says: if $y=\sum_j b_jf_j$ satisfies $B(e_i,y)=0$ for all $i$, then $y=0$. Since $B(e_i,y)=\sum_j\mu_{ij}b_j$, this is $Mb=0\Rightarrow b=0$, so $\operatorname{rank}M=n$ and $n\le m$.

Therefore $m=n$ and $M$ is an invertible $m\times m$ matrix. Finally, $\Phi_B:V\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(W,K)=W^{\vee}$ has matrix $M$ with respect to the basis $(e_i)$ of $V$ and the dual basis $(f_j^{\vee})$ of $W^{\vee}$: indeed $\Phi_B(x)=\sum_j B(x,f_j)\,f_j^{\vee}$, and $B(x,f_j)=\sum_i a_i\mu_{ij}$, so the coordinate vector of $\Phi_B(x)$ is $a^{t}M$. As $M$ is invertible, $a\mapsto a^{t}M$ is a bijection $K^{m}\to K^{m}$, so $\Phi_B$ is a $K$-linear isomorphism. This proves the claim. $\square$ (In particular the claim shows $\dim_K V=\dim_K W$.)

\textbf{Step 3: apply the claim to $B_a$.} Take $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $L=\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ (one-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$), $V=V_a$, $W=W_{2d-a}$, $B=B_a$, all justified by Step 1. The claim yields a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
\Phi_a:V_a\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(W_{2d-a},\,\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\bigr),\qquad \Phi_a(x)(y)=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y).
\]

\textbf{Step 4: identify the composite with the cup-product map.} Since $\operatorname{tr}:T\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism, post-composition with $\operatorname{tr}^{-1}$ gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
\Theta:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(W_{2d-a},\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\bigr)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(W_{2d-a},T\bigr),\qquad \psi\longmapsto \operatorname{tr}^{-1}\circ\psi,
\]
whose inverse is post-composition with $\operatorname{tr}$ (these are mutually inverse because $\operatorname{tr}\circ\operatorname{tr}^{-1}=\operatorname{id}$ and $\operatorname{tr}^{-1}\circ\operatorname{tr}=\operatorname{id}$). The composite $\Theta\circ\Phi_a$ is therefore an isomorphism, and for $x\in V_a$ and $y\in W_{2d-a}$,
\[
(\Theta\circ\Phi_a)(x)(y)=\operatorname{tr}^{-1}\bigl(\Phi_a(x)(y)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\bigr)=x\cup y,
\]
where the last equality holds because $x\cup y\in T$ and $\operatorname{tr}^{-1}\circ\operatorname{tr}=\operatorname{id}_T$. Thus $\Theta\circ\Phi_a=\Psi_a$, the map induced by the cup-product pairing. Being a composite of isomorphisms, $\Psi_a$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
\[
H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-a}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell),\,H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr).
\]
Since $a$ was an arbitrary integer (Step 1 supplies the perfect pairing $B_j$ for every $j\in\mathbb Z$, so no restriction on $a$ is needed and no separate vanishing argument in degrees outside $[0,2d]$ is required), the lemma is proved. $\blacksquare$

\emph{Remark on the argument's structure.} The only geometric input is the trace formulation of Poincar\'e duality for the complement of an ample divisor, quoted verbatim from \texttt{Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_admissible_affine_poincare_duality}; everything else is the formal conversion of a perfect pairing into the $\operatorname{Hom}$-form (Step 2), carried out with dual bases and a rank count so that no ambiguity about the direction of $\operatorname{tr}$ vs.\ $\operatorname{tr}^{-1}$ remains (Step 4). No finite-field input is used, and the base field $k$ is arbitrary algebraically closed as required.

statement: Let q=p^a, \ell\neq p, m\ge 1, k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d\ge 2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and Y\subset X a smooth geometrically connected very ample divisor over \mathbb F_{q^m} with immersion i. Fix \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell and write H^n(Z)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Let \xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y), L_X=\xi\cup-, \xi_Y=i^*\xi, L_Y=\xi_Y\cup-. Suppose L_Y^{d-1-n}:H^n(Y)\to H^{2d-2-n}(Y) is an isomorphism for 0\le n\le d-1. Let U=\mathrm{im}(i^*:H^{d-1}(X)\to H^{d-1}(Y))\cap\ker(L_Y:H^{d-1}(Y)\to H^{d+1}(Y)), and suppose the Poincare trace pairing (a,b)\mapsto\mathrm{tr}_Y(a\cup b) on U is nondegenerate. Then L_X^{d-n}:H^n(X)\to H^{2d-n}(X) is an isomorphism for 0\le n\le d.
proof:
Let Q=q^m=p^{am}. We first check that the hypotheses of the cited lemmas are satisfied. A very ample divisor is an effective Cartier divisor; since Y is smooth, geometrically connected and of pure dimension d-1 with d>=2, it is nonempty. Fix the normalized Poincare duality trace tr_Y supplied by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, after the chosen identification Q_l(1)=Q_l. If the hypothesis of the present lemma uses another Poincare trace, then it differs from this normalized one by a nonzero scalar, because lemma_77 identifies H^{2d-2}(Y) with Q_l(1-d), and hence nondegeneracy of the pairing on U is unchanged.

Step 1: degrees n=0,...,d-2. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_553 to X over F_{q^m}, the divisor Y, xi, L_X, xi_Y and L_Y. Its hypothesis is exactly that L_Y^{d-1-r}:H^r(Y)->H^{2d-2-r}(Y) is an isomorphism for every integer r with 0<=r<=d-1. Therefore L_X^{d-r}:H^r(X)->H^{2d-r}(X) is an isomorphism for every integer r with 0<=r<=d-2. This proves the desired statement for n=0,...,d-2.

Step 2: degree n=d-1. Let W=im(i^*:H^{d-1}(X)->H^{d-1}(Y)). By definition U=W cap ker(L_Y:H^{d-1}(Y)->H^{d+1}(Y)). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_middle_lefschetz_reduces_to_primitive_pairing. The assumptions of that lemma are the same as here: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1, and L_Y^{d-1-r}:H^r(Y)->H^{2d-2-r}(Y) is an isomorphism for all 0<=r<=d-1. The lemma states that L_X:H^{d-1}(X)->H^{d+1}(X) is injective if and only if the pairing (a,b)->tr_Y(a cup b) on U is nondegenerate. By hypothesis this pairing is nondegenerate, so L_X is injective.

To upgrade injectivity to surjectivity, apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_333 with the prime power Q=q^m in place of its q. The lemma says that for a smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension d over F_Q and a very ample divisor Y over F_Q, the map L_X^{d-r}:H^r(X)->H^{2d-r}(X) is injective if and only if it is surjective for every integer r with 0<=r<=d. Taking r=d-1 gives that L_X:H^{d-1}(X)->H^{d+1}(X) is injective if and only if it is surjective. Since we have just proved injectivity, it is surjective, hence an isomorphism.

Step 3: degree n=d. The exponent d-n is 0, so L_X^0 is the identity map on H^d(X), which is an isomorphism.

Combining Steps 1, 2 and 3, L_X^{d-n}:H^n(X)->H^{2d-n}(X) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let B:V\times V\to K be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form with B(v,v)\neq 0 for every nonzero v\in V, and let T\in\mathrm{GL}(V), c\in K^\times satisfy B(Tv,Tw)=cB(v,w) for all v,w\in V. Then T is semisimple on V.
proof:
We prove that T is semisimple by showing that its unipotent Jordan--Chevalley part is the identity.

Step 0 (trivial case). If V = {0}, then T = id_V and its minimal polynomial is t - 1, which is squarefree, so T is semisimple. Henceforth assume V \neq {0}. (The hypothesis B(v,v) \neq 0 for nonzero v is then vacuous in the zero case and is used below only for nonzero vectors.)

Step 1 (B is a perfect pairing). By definition, "nondegenerate" means: B(v,w) = 0 for all w \in V implies v = 0, and (by symmetry, the same holds in the second slot). Consider the K-linear map \varphi: V \to V^{\vee} = \operatorname{Hom}_K(V,K), v \mapsto B(v,\cdot). Nondegeneracy says \ker\varphi = 0, so \varphi is injective; since V is finite dimensional, \dim_K V^{\vee} = \dim_K V, hence \varphi is an isomorphism. Thus B is a perfect K-bilinear form. In particular T has an adjoint T^{*} \in \operatorname{End}_K(V) characterised by B(Tv,w) = B(v,T^{*}w) for all v,w, and the map A \mapsto A^{*} is a K-linear anti-involution of \operatorname{End}_K(V): (AB)^{*} = B^{*}A^{*}, (A+B)^{*} = A^{*}+B^{*}, and A^{*} = 0 implies A = 0 (perfection).

Step 2 (Jordan--Chevalley decomposition). Since char K = 0, the (multiplicative) Jordan--Chevalley decomposition applies to T \in \operatorname{GL}_K(V): there exist unique commuting operators T_s, T_u \in \operatorname{End}_K(V) with T = T_s T_u = T_u T_s, with T_s semisimple (its minimal polynomial over K is squarefree, equivalently T_s \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalisable over an algebraic closure \bar K) and T_u unipotent (T_u = \mathrm{id} + N with N nilpotent; in particular T_u \in \operatorname{GL}_K(V)). Concretely, factoring the minimal polynomial \mu_T = \prod_j f_j^{e_j} into powers of distinct monic irreducibles (which are separable because char K = 0) gives the T-stable primary decomposition V = \bigoplus_j \ker f_j(T)^{e_j}; on \ker f_j(T)^{e_j} the operator T_s is the unique semisimple operator with minimal polynomial f_j, and T_u = T T_s^{-1} there, which is \mathrm{id} plus a nilpotent. Both T_s and T_u lie in the commutative subalgebra K[T,T^{-1}] \subset \operatorname{End}_K(V). We record that T_u is invertible and unipotent, as required to apply the lemmas quoted below.

Step 3 (the unipotent part is a B-isometry). We apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_495 with the perfect bilinear form \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle := B (Step 1), the scalar c \in K^{\times}, and the similitude T (hypothesis B(Tv,Tw) = c\,B(v,w) for all v,w). That lemma asserts precisely that the two factors of the Jordan decomposition are again similitudes of B, with multipliers c and 1 respectively; the second assertion gives
   B(T_u v, T_u w) = B(v,w) \qquad \text{for all } v,w \in V.
(For orientation, the mechanism is that the anti-involution A \mapsto A^{*} restricts to the commutative algebra K[T,T^{-1}] and sends T to cT^{-1} = (cT_s^{-1})\cdot T_u^{-1}, a product of a semisimple and a commuting unipotent operator; by uniqueness of the Jordan decomposition one gets T_u^{*} = T_u^{-1}, whence B(T_uv,T_uw) = B(v,T_u^{*}T_uw) = B(v,w). The lemma is already proved, so we rely on it.)

Step 4 (an anisotropic-form isometry that is unipotent is trivial). The form B is symmetric and satisfies B(v,v) \neq 0 for every nonzero v \in V, exactly the hypothesis of the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_520, which states: over a field of characteristic 0, a unipotent U \in \operatorname{GL}(V) preserving such a B is the identity. Applying it to U := T_u (unipotent by Step 2, a B-isometry by Step 3) yields
   T_u = \mathrm{id}_V.

Step 5 (conclusion). From Step 2, T = T_s T_u = T_s \circ \mathrm{id}_V = T_s. Since T_s is semisimple, T is semisimple on V. Equivalently, the minimal polynomial \mu_T is squarefree in K[t] (had T_u = \mathrm{id} + N with N \neq 0 nilpotent, some primary component would have repeated factor, contradicting Step 4), and T \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalisable on V \otimes_K \bar K.

This completes the proof for all V, including V = \{0\}. Note that no property of the multiplier c beyond c \in K^{\times} was needed, and the symmetry of B was used only through the anisotropy hypothesis B(v,v) \neq 0 in Step 4.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor, let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and let \(\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\) be the trace pairing on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(A\subset H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all divisors on \(S_k\). Suppose \(\beta|_A\) is nondegenerate. Then \(P^2=\ker(L:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\) is the direct sum \((A\cap P^2)\oplus A^\perp\).
proof:
Write V := H^2_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and W := H^4_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); both are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. The chosen nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) gives identifications \mathbb Q_\ell(\pm 2)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell, and via them the trace of the statement is the map \operatorname{tr}_S:W\to\mathbb Q_\ell and the pairing is \beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y) on V.

We use the following geometric input, which is exactly the case Y=S, d=2, n=2 of the Poincar\'e duality lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 (S is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q, \ell\neq p):
(PD-a) the cycle-class/Gysin construction gives an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces \operatorname{tr}_S:H^4_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-2), hence, after the fixed identification of Tate twists with \mathbb Q_\ell, the map \operatorname{tr}_S:W\to\mathbb Q_\ell is an isomorphism;
(PD-b) for every n the pairing H^n_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{4-n}_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-2), (x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y), is perfect; in particular for n=2 the pairing \beta:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_\ell is perfect, i.e. the two maps V\to V^{\vee}, x\mapsto\beta(x,-) and x\mapsto\beta(-,x), are isomorphisms.

Step 0 (symmetry). The \acute etale cohomology ring of S_k is graded-commutative, and both arguments of \beta lie in degree 2, so \beta(y,x)=(-1)^{2\cdot 2}\beta(x,y)=\beta(x,y). Thus \beta is symmetric, and for a subspace E\subset V the left and right orthogonal complements coincide; we write E^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\beta(e,v)=0\ \forall e\in E\} without ambiguity.

Step 1 (the class \xi lies in A). By hypothesis \xi is the cycle class in H^2_{\acute et}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) of an \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor H\subset S. Cycle classes of Cartier divisors are compatible with the base change S\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m} along \operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m} (flat base change for the Gysin/cycle-class class map of a relative effective Cartier divisor), so \xi is precisely the cycle class of the divisor H_k on the k-scheme S_k. Since A is by definition the \mathbb Q_\ell-span of the cycle classes of all divisors on S_k, we get
\qquad \xi\in A. \quad (1)

Step 2 (P^2 is the orthogonal line complement of \xi). For x\in V, using commutativity of the even-degree parts of the cohomology ring,
\qquad \beta(x,\xi)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup\xi)=\operatorname{tr}_S(\xi\cup x)=\operatorname{tr}_S(Lx). \quad (2)
Because \operatorname{tr}_S:W\to\mathbb Q_\ell is an isomorphism by (PD-a), \operatorname{tr}_S(Lx)=0 if and only if Lx=0. Hence, by the definition P^2=\ker(L:V\to W) and by (2),
\qquad x\in P^2\iff Lx=0\iff \operatorname{tr}_S(Lx)=0\iff \beta(x,\xi)=0,
that is,
\qquad P^2=\xi^{\perp}. \quad (3)

Step 3 (A^{\perp}\subset P^2). If x\in A^{\perp} then \beta(x,a)=0 for every a\in A; by (1) the element \xi belongs to A, so \beta(x,\xi)=0, and (3) gives x\in P^2. Thus
\qquad A^{\perp}\subset P^2. \quad (4)

Step 4 (V=A\oplus A^{\perp}). Consider the linear map \varphi:V\to A^{\vee} defined by \varphi(x)(a)=\beta(a,x). The map V\to V^{\vee}, x\mapsto\beta(-,x), is an isomorphism by the perfectness (PD-b), and the restriction map V^{\vee}\to A^{\vee} is surjective (every linear form on a subspace of a vector space extends to the whole space); hence \varphi is surjective and \dim\ker\varphi=\dim V-\dim A. But \ker\varphi=A^{\perp} by definition. On the other hand A\cap A^{\perp}=\operatorname{rad}(\beta|_A)=\{0\} because \beta|_A is nondegenerate by hypothesis. Therefore
\qquad \dim(A+A^{\perp})=\dim A+\dim A^{\perp}=\dim A+(\dim V-\dim A)=\dim V,
so V=A\oplus A^{\perp}.

Step 5 (P^2\subset (A\cap P^2)+A^{\perp}). Let x\in P^2. By Step 4 write x=a+b uniquely with a\in A and b\in A^{\perp}. By (4), b\in P^2; since P^2 is a \mathbb Q_\ell-subspace, a=x-b\in P^2. Hence a\in A\cap P^2, so x\in (A\cap P^2)+A^{\perp}.

Step 6 (the sum is direct). (A\cap P^2)\cap A^{\perp}\subset A\cap A^{\perp}=\{0\} by Step 4.

Combining Steps 3, 5 and 6 we obtain
\qquad P^2=(A\cap P^2)\oplus A^{\perp},
which is exactly the claimed decomposition. \hfill\blacksquare

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), and let \(\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_S(x\cup y)\) be the trace pairing on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(F\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(A\) be the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-span of the cycle classes of all divisors on \(S_k\), and let \(T=A^\perp\) with respect to \(\beta\). Then \(F(A)\subseteq A\) and \(F(T)\subseteq T\).
proof:
Write V := H^2_et(S_k, Q_ell). Fix the given nonzero element of Q_ell(1), which identifies every Tate twist Q_ell(j) with Q_ell; all cycle classes below are taken under this identification, as in the statement. Let sigma_m : k -> k, sigma_m(u) = u^{q^m}, and let tau := id_{S_k} x Spec sigma_m, so that F = tau^* is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius of V.

Step 1: V is finite-dimensional, and beta is a perfect pairing satisfying the Frobenius quasi-invariance.
Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 with Y = S, which is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d = 2 over F_{q^m}, and with n = 2 (so 2d - n = 2). Its part (b) says that (x,y) |-> tr_S(x cup y), viewed as a pairing with values in Q_ell(-2), is PERFECT, and that <Fx, Fy> = q^{m*2}<x,y> for all x,y. Composing with the fixed Q_ell-linear isomorphism Q_ell(-2) ~-> Q_ell supplied by the chosen nonzero element of Q_ell(1) gives exactly the pairing beta of the statement; hence
   (1) beta is a perfect Q_ell-bilinear form on V, and
   (2) beta(Fx, Fy) = q^{2m} beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.
Perfectness implies dim_{Q_ell} V < infinity: indeed V ~-> V^* by (1), and a vector space canonically isomorphic to its own dual is finite-dimensional (an infinite-dimensional W has dim W^* > dim W, so W -> W^{**} is not surjective). Consequently every Q_ell-subspace of V, and in particular A, is finite-dimensional. Applying (2) with x = F^{-1}x', y = F^{-1}y' (F is an automorphism of V by lemma_77) gives
   (3) beta(F^{-1}x', F^{-1}y') = q^{-2m} beta(x',y') for all x',y' in V.

Step 2: F(A) subseteq A.
A is by definition the Q_ell-span of the classes cl(D) of all divisors D on S_k, so it suffices to show F(cl(D)) in A for each such D.

Step 2a (descent of a divisor to a finite extension). Let D = sum_i n_i Z_i be a divisor on S_k, with the Z_i distinct integral closed subschemes of codimension 1 and n_i in Z. Since S is of finite type over F_{q^m}, S_k is noetherian, so D has only finitely many components. Each Z_i is a closed subscheme of the k-scheme S_k of finite type, hence is defined by a coherent ideal sheaf I_i on S_k; coherent sheaves and the relations among finitely many of their local generators are defined over a finitely generated Q_ell-free... more precisely, by standard noetherian approximation/descent for coherent sheaves on a scheme of finite type over a field, there is a finitely generated Z_i0 := Spec? — concretely, there is a finitely generated F_{q^m}-subalgebra R_i of k over which I_i is the base change of a coherent ideal of S_{R_i}. Since k is algebraic over F_{q^m}, every finitely generated F_{q^m}-subalgebra of k is a field, a finite extension of F_{q^m}. Choose a finite extension k'/F_{q^m} inside k containing all the R_i (finitely many of them). Then each Z_i descends to a closed subscheme of S_{k'}, flat base change to S_k recovering Z_i, and thus D descends to a codimension-1 cycle z on S_{k'} (equivalently, a divisor on S_k defined over the finite extension k' of F_{q^m}) whose base change to k is D. Because the cycle class map is compatible with flat base change, the class c_z in H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) attached to z over k' is exactly cl(D).

Step 2b (apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/142de9). That lemma applies verbatim: X = S is smooth projective over F_{q^m}, k is an algebraic closure of F_q, j = 1, sigma_m(u) = u^{q^m}, tau = id x Spec sigma_m, F = tau^*, and z is a codimension-1 cycle on S_k defined over the finite extension k'/F_{q^m}. It yields a scalar lambda in Q_ell^x with
   F(cl(D)) = F(c_z) = lambda * c_{tau^{-1}z},
where tau^{-1}z denotes the inverse-image cycle. Since sigma_m is an automorphism of k, tau is an automorphism of S_k, so tau^{-1}z is again a divisor on S_k; hence c_{tau^{-1}z} is one of the generators of A, and F(cl(D)) = lambda c_{tau^{-1}z} in A. As every element of A is a finite Q_ell-linear combination of such generators cl(D) and F is Q_ell-linear, F(A) subseteq A.

Step 3: F^{-1}(A) = A.
The restriction F|_A : A -> A is Q_ell-linear and injective (F is an automorphism of V). Since A is finite-dimensional (Step 1), an injective endomorphism of A is surjective, so F(A) = A; equivalently F^{-1}(A) = A. In particular, for every a in A one has F^{-1}a in A.

Step 4: F(T) subseteq T.
Let t in T = A^perp and a in A. By Step 3, F^{-1}a in A, and since t is orthogonal to every element of A, beta(t, F^{-1}a) = 0. Therefore, using (2),
   beta(Ft, a) = beta(Ft, F(F^{-1}a)) = q^{2m} beta(t, F^{-1}a) = 0.
As a ranged over all of A, this says Ft in A^perp = T. Hence F(T) subseteq T.

Steps 2 and 4 give the two required inclusions, F(A) subseteq A and F(T) subseteq T. This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(m\ge 1\) be an integer, let \(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_m\in\mathbb C\) be nonzero complex numbers, put \(R=\max_{1\le j\le m}|\beta_j|\), and let \(r=\#\{j:|\beta_j|=R\}\). Then there is a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) such that \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_j^{n_k}R^{-n_k}\to r\) as \(k\to\infty\).
proof:
We prove the statement with the limit equal to \(r=\#\{j:|\beta_j|=R\}\). (This is the corrected constant; when \(r=m\) — e.g. all \(\beta_j\) of equal modulus, as for the eigenvalues of a pure Frobenius — the conclusion reads \(\to m\).)

**Step 0: Normalisation and elementary facts.** Since \(m\ge 1\) and every \(\beta_j\neq 0\), each \(|\beta_j|>0\), so \(R=\max_j|\beta_j|\ge|\beta_1|>0\). The maximum is attained (finite set), so \(r\ge 1\). Put
\[u_j=\beta_j/R\in\mathbb C,\qquad |u_j|\le 1\ \ \forall j,\]
and set \(M=\{j\in\{1,\dots,m\}:|u_j|=1\}\); then \(\#M=r\ge 1\) and \(|u_j|<1\) for \(j\notin M\). Finally \(\beta_j^{n}R^{-n}=(\beta_j/R)^n=u_j^{n}\), so it suffices to construct strictly increasing positive integers \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^m u_j^{n_k}\to r\).

**Step 1: A return lemma on the torus (\(*\)).** Let \(\mathbb T=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}\), and put on \(\mathbb T^{\rho}\) (\(\rho\ge 1\)) the metric \(d(a,b)=\max_{i}|a_i-b_i|\). This metric induces the product topology, is translation invariant (\(d(ac,bc)=d(a,b)\) since \(|c_i|=1\)), and \(\mathbb T^{\rho}\) is compact (closed and bounded in \(\mathbb C^{\rho}\cong\mathbb R^{2\rho}\), Heine–Borel).

**Claim (\(*\)).** For every \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_\rho)\in\mathbb T^{\rho}\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every \(N\ge 1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(\max_i|x_i^{n}-1|<\varepsilon\).

*Proof of (1a) — arbitrarily small steps.* Given \(\delta>0\) we produce \(d\ge 1\) with \(d(x^{d},1)<\delta\). If the cyclic subgroup \(\{x^{n}:n\in\mathbb Z\}\) is finite of exponent \(L\ge 1\), take \(d=L\) and \(x^{d}=1\). Otherwise the points \(x^{0},x^{1},\dots,x^{K}\) are pairwise distinct for arbitrarily large \(K\). Cover the compact metric space \(\mathbb T^{\rho}\) by finitely many open balls of radius \(\delta/2\) (total boundedness); say \(K\) balls. For this \(K\), two of the \(K+1\) points \(x^{n_1},x^{n_2}\) (\(0\le n_1<n_2\le K\)) lie in a common ball, so \(d(x^{n_1},x^{n_2})<\delta\). By translation invariance with \(c=x^{-n_1}\) (componentwise inverse, still in \(\mathbb T^{\rho}\)), \(d(x^{d},1)<\delta\) for \(d=n_2-n_1\ge 1\).

*Proof of (1b) — late returns.* Fix \(d\ge 1\) from (1a) and write \(s=x^{d}\), \(\Gamma=\{s^{q}:q\in\mathbb Z\}\), \(H'=\overline{\Gamma}\) (a compact subgroup of \(\mathbb T^{\rho}\), the closure of a subgroup of an abelian topological group). For \(Q\ge 0\) set \(A_Q=\overline{\{s^{q}:q\ge Q\}}\); these are nonempty compact sets, decreasing in \(Q\). Let \(A=\bigcap_{Q\ge 0}A_Q\neq\varnothing\) (nested nonempty compact sets). Multiplication by \(s\) is a homeomorphism, so \(A_Qs=\overline{\{s^{q}:q\ge Q+1\}}=A_{Q+1}\subseteq A_Q\); hence \(As\subseteq A\). The sets \(A s^{Q}\) (\(Q\ge 0\)) are nonempty compact and decreasing, so \(B=\bigcap_{Q\ge 0}As^{Q}\neq\varnothing\), and
\[ Bs=\Big(\bigcap_{Q\ge 0}As^{Q}\Big)s=\bigcap_{Q\ge 0}As^{Q+1}=\bigcap_{Q\ge 1}As^{Q}=B,\]
where the first equality uses that \(z\mapsto zs\) is a homeomorphism (so it commutes with intersections) and the last uses that dropping the first term of a decreasing sequence does not change the intersection. Thus \(Bs=B\), which gives invariance under \(s\) and under \(s^{-1}\) (if \(b\in B=\Bs\) then \(b=zs\) with \(z\in B\), so \(bs^{-1}=z\in B\)), hence \(B\gamma=B\) for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). Since \(B\subseteq A\subseteq \overline{\{s^{q}:q\ge 0\}}\subseteq H'\) and \(B\) is closed, invariance extends by limits to all of \(H'\): for \(h\in H'\), \(h=\lim_k\gamma_k\) with \(\gamma_k\in\Gamma\), and \(bh=\lim_k b\gamma_k\in B\). Therefore \(bH'\subseteq B\) for each \(b\in B\), and conversely \(B=b(b^{-1}B)\subseteq bH'\) because \(b^{-1}B\subseteq H'\). So \(B=bH'\); as \(b\in B\subseteq H'\) and \(H'\) is a group, \(bH'=H'\), i.e. \(B=H'\). In particular \(1\in B\subseteq A_Q\) for every \(Q\ge 0\): \(1\in\overline{\{s^{q}:q\ge Q\}}\) for all \(Q\).

*Proof of (1c) — conclusion of (\(*\)).* Given \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(N\ge 1\): choose \(d\ge 1\) by (1a) (any \(d\)), let \(s=x^d\), pick \(Q\) with \(Qd\ge N\), and use \(1\in\overline{\{s^{q}:q\ge Q\}}\) to find \(q\ge Q\) with \(d(s^{q},1)=\max_i|x_i^{qd}-1|<\varepsilon\). Then \(n=qd\ge N\) works. This proves (\(*\)).

**Step 2: Decay of the non-maximal terms.** If \(M\neq\{1,\dots,m\}\), set \(\rho=\max_{j\notin M}|u_j|\). The set is nonempty and each \(|u_j|\in(0,1)\) (strictly positive because \(\beta_j\neq 0\)), so \(0<\rho<1\) and \(\rho^{n}\to 0\). Hence for each \(k\ge 1\) there is a threshold \(T_k\) with \(\rho^{n}<1/(km)\) for all \(n\ge T_k\); explicitly \(T_k=\lfloor \log(km)/\log(1/\rho)\rfloor+2\) works. If \(M=\{1,\dots,m\}\) the complementary sum below is empty and we set \(T_k=k\). In both cases \(T_k\to\infty\).

**Step 3: Diagonal construction of the sequence.** Enumerate \(M=\{j_1<\dots<j_r\}\) and apply (\(*\)) to \(x=(u_{j_1},\dots,u_{j_r})\in\mathbb T^{r}\) (legal since \(r\ge 1\)). Define \(n_k\) recursively: given \(n_{k-1}\) (with \(n_0=0\)), apply (\(*\)) with \(\varepsilon=1/k\) and \(N_k=\max(n_{k-1}+1,\,T_k)\) to obtain an integer \(n_k\ge N_k\) with
\[ \max_{j\in M}\bigl|u_j^{\,n_k}-1\bigr|<\frac1k .\]
Then \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) are strictly increasing positive integers, \(n_k\ge T_k\) (so \(\rho^{n_k}<1/(km)\) in the case \(M\subsetneq\{1,\dots,m\}\)), and the displayed estimate holds.

**Step 4: The estimate.** Decompose the sum into maximal and non-maximal terms, and subtract \(r=\sum_{j\in M}1\) (this is where the count \(r\), not \(m\), enters):
\[ \sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j^{\,n_k}-r=\sum_{j\in M}\bigl(u_j^{\,n_k}-1\bigr)+\sum_{j\notin M}u_j^{\,n_k}. \]
Indeed the right-hand side equals \(\bigl(\sum_{j\in M}u_j^{n_k}-r\bigr)+\sum_{j\notin M}u_j^{n_k}=\sum_{j=1}^m u_j^{n_k}-r\). Taking absolute values and using the triangle inequality,
\[ \Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j^{\,n_k}-r\Bigr|\le\sum_{j\in M}\bigl|u_j^{\,n_k}-1\bigr|+\sum_{j\notin M}\bigl|u_j\bigr|^{n_k}\le \frac{r}{k}+(m-r)\rho^{n_k}\le \frac{r}{k}+m\cdot\frac{1}{km}=\frac{r+1}{k},\]
where in the middle we used \(\#M=r\) terms each bounded by \(1/k\), and the last inequality is \(\sum_{j\notin M}|u_j|^{n_k}\le (m-r)\rho^{n_k}\le m\rho^{n_k}<1/k\) (with the convention that the sum is \(0\) when \(M=\{1,\dots,m\}\), in which case the bound is trivial). If \(M\subsetneq\{1,\dots,m\}\) this uses \(n_k\ge T_k\); if \(M=\{1,\dots,m\}\) the second sum is empty and the same bound holds. Since \((r+1)/k\to 0\), we obtain \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j^{\,n_k}\to r\).

**Step 5: Conclusion.** As \(\beta_j^{n_k}R^{-n_k}=u_j^{\,n_k}\) for every \(j\) and \(k\), Step 4 gives
\[ \sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_j^{n_k}R^{-n_k}\longrightarrow r=\#\{j:|\beta_j|=R\},\]
for the strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) constructed in Step 3. \(\blacksquare\)

*Remark on the correction.* The earlier value \(m\) is wrong in general: for \(m=2\), \(\beta_1=1\), \(\beta_2=1/2\) one has \(R=1\) and \(\beta_1^{n}+\beta_2^{n}\to 1=r\) along every sequence \(n\to\infty\), never \(2\). The argument above yields the correct limit \(r\), and recovers \(m\) exactly when all \(|\beta_j|=R\).

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Suppose the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(i\ge0\) and on \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(j\ge0\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
proof:
Write $Q:=q^m=p^{am}$, so that $Q$ is again a prime power and $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q$. The endomorphism whose semisimplicity is hypothesised and concluded is, in every case, the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^Q=c^{q^m}$. Thus, after the harmless renaming $Q\leftrightarrow q$, the statement we must prove is: for smooth projective geometrically connected varieties $X,Y$ over $\mathbb F_Q$ such that the $Q$-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on $H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $i\ge0$ and on $H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $j\ge0$, the same Frobenius is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $n\ge0$. We prove this formulation; it is literally identical to the required one.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ for the rest of the argument; since $n$ is arbitrary, what follows will give the result for every $n$.

**Step 1: finite-dimensionality of the factors.** $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective over $\mathbb F_Q$, hence proper. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (with $\mathbb F_Q$ in place of its $\mathbb F_q$, and with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf, which carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) to $X$ and to $Y$, we obtain that for every $i\ge0$ and $j\ge0$ the spaces
$$H^i:=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad H^j(Y):=H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$$
are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces (and likewise $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, since $X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y$ is again proper over $\mathbb F_Q$).

**Step 2: the Frobenius operators are invertible.** By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied over $\mathbb F_Q$), for each $Z\in\{X,Y,X\times Y\}$ the pullback $F_Z:=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^Q$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^t_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $t\ge0$ (its inverse being the $Q$-power geometric Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$). We write $F_X^{(t)}$ and $F_Y^{(t)}$ for the restrictions of $F_X,F_Y$ to $H^t$ and $H^t(Y)$; these are elements of $\mathrm{GL}$ of the respective spaces.

**Step 3: each tensor factor is semisimple.** Consider the finite index set $I_n:=\{(i,j)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:\ i+j=n\}$ (it has exactly $n+1$ elements). For each $(i,j)\in I_n$ set $V_{i,j}:=H^i\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j(Y)$, a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space by Step 1, and $T_{i,j}:=F_X^{(i)}\otimes F_Y^{(j)}\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V_{i,j})$. By hypothesis $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^i$ and $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^j(Y)$. Since $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_590 applies to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, $V=H^i$, $W=H^j(Y)$, $T=F_X^{(i)}$, $S=F_Y^{(j)}$ and yields that $T_{i,j}$ is semisimple on $V_{i,j}$, for every $(i,j)\in I_n$.

**Step 4: the direct sum of the factors is semisimple.** Put $W_n:=\bigoplus_{(i,j)\in I_n}V_{i,j}$ and $S_n:=\bigoplus_{(i,j)\in I_n}T_{i,j}\in\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W_n)$. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (with $m=|I_n|=n+1$, $V_{i,j}$ as the summands and $T_{i,j}$ as the operators), $S_n$ is semisimple if and only if each $T_{i,j}$ is; Step 3 gives the latter, hence $S_n$ is semisimple on $W_n$.

**Step 5: transport across the Künneth isomorphism.** Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 with $\mathbb F_Q$ in place of its $\mathbb F_q$, to the smooth projective varieties $X$ and $Y$ (geometric connectedness is not needed there) and to the fixed degree $n$. It gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism
$$\kappa_n:\ \bigoplus_{i+j=n}H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ {\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }}\ H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*(x)\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*(y),$$
where $\mathrm{pr}_1,\mathrm{pr}_2$ are the two projections, and it states that under $\kappa_n$ the operator $F_{X\times Y}$ on the target corresponds to $F_X\otimes F_Y$ on the $(i,j)$-summand for all $i,j$. Identifying $W_n$ with the source of $\kappa_n$ (they are the same direct sum, and $\kappa_n$ is defined summandwise), this is precisely the intertwining relation
$$\kappa_n\circ S_n \;=\; F_{X\times Y}^{(n)}\circ\kappa_n .$$
Indeed both sides send a simple tensor $x\otimes y$ with $x\in H^i$, $y\in H^j$, $i+j=n$, to $\mathrm{pr}_1^*(F_X^{(i)}x)\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*(F_Y^{(j)}y)$: for the left-hand side this is the definition of $\kappa_n$ applied to $F_X^{(i)}x\otimes F_Y^{(j)}y$, and for the right-hand side it is the functoriality of pull-back together with the compatibility of the Künneth map with $Q$-power Frobenius, which is exactly the content of the cited lemma (its proof rests on eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, i.e. on the fact that $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ F_{X\times Y}=F_X\circ\mathrm{pr}_1$ and $\mathrm{pr}_2\circ F_{X\times Y}=F_Y\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$ as morphisms over the field automorphism $\sigma$, and on the fact that $F^*$ is a ring homomorphism for the cup product).

**Step 6: conclusion for degree $n$.** The spaces $W_n$ and $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (Steps 1 and 5), the operators $S_n$ and $F_{X\times Y}^{(n)}$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms (Step 2), and they are intertwined by the isomorphism $\kappa_n$ (Step 5). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, $S_n$ is semisimple if and only if $F_{X\times Y}^{(n)}$ is semisimple. Step 4 gives semisimplicity of $S_n$, hence $F_{X\times Y}$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

**Step 7: remove the renaming and vary $n$.** Reverting $Q=q^m$, the operator just treated is $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ with $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$, i.e. the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k)$, and $X\times_{\mathbb F_Q}Y=X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y$. Since $n\ge0$ was arbitrary, this Frobenius is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge0$, which is the desired conclusion. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(m\ge1\), let \(m'\ge1\) be a multiple of \(m\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(S\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). For \(r\in\{m,m'\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_r:H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be the Poincar\'e duality trace of \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\), normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_r(\operatorname{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_{q^r}]\) for every closed point \(z\) of \(S_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}_m=\operatorname{tr}_{m'}\).
proof:
Let F_r denote F_{q^r}. For r=m,m' put S_r = S x_{F_m} F_r. Since S is smooth projective geometrically connected over F_m, each S_r is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 2 over F_r: smoothness and projectivity are stable under base change, and (S_r) x_{F_r} k = S x_{F_m} k is connected because S is geometrically connected over F_m. Fix the given identification of Tate twists with Q_l, and write cl(x) for the class in H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) of a closed point x of S_r, obtained from the usual codimension-2 cycle class by this fixed identification.

By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, applied to Y=S_r, there is a Q_l-linear Poincare duality trace isomorphism T_r: H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) -> Q_l (after the fixed identification Q_l(-2)=Q_l) such that for every closed point x of S_r, T_r(cl(x)) = [kappa(x):F_r]. The traces tr_r in the statement are normalized in the same way.

Choose a closed point z of S over F_m; such a point exists because S is nonempty of finite type over a field. Let n = [kappa(z):F_m] >= 1. Then kappa(z) is a finite field of cardinality q^{mn}. By the normalization for tr_m, tr_m(cl(z)) = n. In particular n is nonzero in Q_l, so cl(z) is nonzero. Since T_m is an isomorphism, H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) is one-dimensional; hence cl(z) is a basis. Therefore two Q_l-linear maps from H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) to Q_l are equal if they agree on cl(z).

It remains to compute tr_{m'}(cl(z)). View z as a closed subscheme of S_{m'} after base change: z_{m'} = z x_{F_m} F_{m'}. The base change of z_{m'} to k is canonically the same closed subscheme z x_{F_m} k of S_k. Hence the cycle class of z as a 0-cycle on S_{m'} (after base change to k) is the same element cl(z) of H^4_et(S_k,Q_l).

Write m' = m s with s >= 1. Since kappa(z) = F_{mn}, we have kappa(z) tensor_{F_m} F_{m'} = F_{mn} tensor_{F_m} F_{ms}. For finite fields, F_{q^A} tensor_{F_{q^B}} F_{q^C} with B|A,C is a product of gcd(A/B,C/B) copies of F_{q^{lcm(A,C)}}. Applying this with A=mn, B=m, C=ms gives F_{mn} tensor_{F_m} F_{ms} = product_{i=1}^{g} F_{m l}, where g = gcd(n,s) and l = lcm(n,s). Equivalently, the tensor product is finite etale of rank n over F_{ms}; its geometric points are the n embeddings of F_{mn} into k over F_m, grouped into Gal(k/F_{ms})-orbits of size l/s, hence there are g=n/(l/s)=gcd(n,s) factors.

Thus z_{m'} is a disjoint union of g closed points z'_1,...,z'_g of S_{m'}, each with residue field F_{ml}. For each i, [kappa(z'_i):F_{m'}] = [F_{ml}:F_{ms}] = l/s. By additivity of cycle classes for disjoint unions, cl(z) = sum_{i=1}^{g} cl(z'_i). By the normalization of tr_{m'} for closed points of S_{m'}, tr_{m'}(cl(z'_i)) = l/s. Therefore tr_{m'}(cl(z)) = sum_{i=1}^{g} l/s = g l/s = gcd(n,s) lcm(n,s)/s = n, because gcd(n,s) lcm(n,s) = n s.

Thus tr_m(cl(z)) = n = tr_{m'}(cl(z)). Since cl(z) is a basis of H^4_et(S_k,Q_l) and both traces are Q_l-linear maps to Q_l, tr_m = tr_{m'}.
